Noble Audio's Astrid have a triple-driver system and sleek looks .

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Noble Audio has had one seriously busy year in 2026, and it's not over yet. The Texas-based company has impressed us with in-ear monitors and over-ear cans alike, from the Lu Ban wired IEMs made from cocobolo wood to the Noble FoKus Artemis over-ear ANC headphones, which we gave a near-perfect 4.5-star review.

Now, it's adding another wireless in-ear headphone to its lineup. The Astrid will sit somewhere in the middle of its current offering, so they won't enter our pick of the best budget IEMs, but they offer an intriguing proposition: three driver technologies for the ability to both adapt sound to your own unique hearing profile and adjust it to how you want it to sound.

They look sharp too with an intricate silver-toned frost-like pattern over the glass fiber earbud and the charging case.

Hybrid earphones are a familiar territory for Noble Audio, which has explored driver combinations in its universal and custom in-ear monitors. Astrid brings that experience to a new wireless design.

There are three driver technologies in each ear piece: an 8.3mm dynamic driver, 6mm planar driver and a balanced armature. The first uses a PU diaphragm with an aluminium-magnesium alloy dome. This works alongside the other two technologies in a hybrid system that takes account of differences between your left and right ears as well as the way your hearing differs from other people’s.

Using Audiodo Personal Sound, a short test checks each ear and creates a personal hearing profile. This is then used to adjust playback to your ears. Meanwhile, the Audiodo Equalizer allows you to adjust bass, mids and treble as preferred: the result is sound that accounts for both how you hear and how you like your music to sound, the company says.

The new TWS has Active Noise Cancellation and a Transparency mode to let through outside sound when needed. Microphone noise and wind reduction are intended to help with calls, while Bluetooth 6.0 and two-device multipoint make it possible to keep a phone and laptop connected at the same time.

Noble cites up to 11 hours of listening per charge and up to 40 hours including the case, depending on settings, with USB-C and wireless charging. There's a choice of silicone ear tips, and the buds have IPX4 splash resistance.

Priced at $539 / £499, the Astrid sits above the $200 Osprey and the Rex5 but below the flagship Prestige Encore II in Noble's growing TWS range. You can order at nobleaudio.com and selected retailers.

#9131. Six standout projects unveiled at Designart Tokyo 2026

As the 10th anniversary edition of Designart Tokyo gets underway, Jane Englefield reports on six highlights from the citywide festival of Japanese creativity.

Designart Tokyo opened on 30 October and will remain open across Tokyo until 8 November.

Around 150 projects by exhibitors from 13 countries are on display at various galleries and other pop-up locations throughout the city.

This year’s main exhibition venue is the former site of the Tokyo Expressway, also known as the KK Line, a portion of which is now an elevated park in the heart of Ginza.

Designart Tokyo’s first dedicated design store is also located on site, selling works from brands including Nendo and Alessi, as well as designers Ronan Bouroullec and Kwangho Lee.

Read on for six of our highlights from the event:

Pulling Apart is a novel adhesive on display as part of the Daikanyama exhibition Separation: Designed to Come Apart, which includes various products created to allow for fluid disassembly and recycling.

Tokyo studio Nomura created the project with the knowledge that, when glue-based adhesives are applied to timber or metal, they are often difficult or impossible to remove. This can mean that materials suffer indelible marks or cannot be recycled at the end of their life.

Nomura’s adhesive is a strong but flexible tape, which firmly holds heavy materials in place. But once the tape is tugged, it stretches and comes away easily.

“Leave one end within reach behind the plinth or under the tabletop, and when the time comes, a single pull undoes the whole thing,” said Nomura.

The tape was developed with easy-disassembly bonding technology developed by Aica Kogyo Company and is still in the prototype phase.

“Peco poco” is a common Japanese onomatopoeia describing a growling stomach.

Experimental design studio Howdunit used the phrase as its starting point for this table lamp, which can be manually unfolded like an accordion thanks to a small hook built into the top of the shade.

Made from delicate layers of gauzy textile, the light opens with a “rhythmic ‘peco poco’ motion” and can be set at various heights.

“By continually asking how things are made, we aim to discover new possibilities in design,” said Howdunit founders Haruto Kamijo and Sho Tasaki.

Forest: Perspectives by Oji Holdings and We+

Tokyo paper manufacturer Oji Holdings is presenting an exhibition in Ginza that meditates on our perspectives on forests.

The manufacturer asked nine professionals, from designers and wood specialists to a writer and a chef, to visit the network of forests it manages and share their individual responses to the landscape.

Among them are delicately whittled spoons made from fallen branches and wood sheets crafted out of bark using a process similar to making washi paper.

The exhibition was laid out in an encyclopedic display designed by local studio We+, founded by Toshiya Hayashi and Hokuto Ando.

Founded in 2021, Tokyo-based 21B Studio is presenting an exhibition at Shibuya’s brutalist-style Tiers Gallery.

Box is the first solo show by the young studio, conceived to demonstrate the myriad ways we can create the humble paper box through various folds and incisions.

The studio is giving out an intricately designed flatpack poster advertising the exhibition, which, once assembled, resembles the geometric architecture of Tiers Gallery itself.

Over in Tokyo Midtown, design master’s student Cecil Nabenashi is presenting a playful exhibition of vases and bowls made of deep-fried paper and fibres.

Nabenashi looked to tempura, Japanese food that is coated in batter and deep-fried in oil, when creating the project.

His goal was to experiment with his “tempura” technique to see if it could provide a long-lasting finish for design objects, using a “batter” he developed from a specially developed blend of non-edible ingredients.

The designer told Dezeen that he plans for his next challenge to be a deep-fried garment.

Industrial Romanticism is an exhibition on display at Minato’s Axis Gallery, Japan’s first dedicated design gallery founded in 1981.

The show is a group exhibition held by designers Yoshiki Matsuyama and Ryota Yokozeki, who asked eight leading Japanese companies to take part.

In-house designers at each of the companies, including bathroom brand Toto and camera maker Fujifilm, created prototypes of recognisable products with an imaginative twist.

Among the designs is a piano made by Ryusuke Baba of musical instrument maker Yamaha. Baba created the piano from pieces of timber that would normally be rejected for an instrument, creating a keyboard with an offbeat sound.

Designart Tokyo 2026 takes place from 30 October to 8 November 2026 at various locations across Tokyo, Japan. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

#9130. Gochman Collection Builds a Home for Native Art in Westchester

The private collection opened its Branchline location in Katonah as a way to bring Native art into public view, though questions linger about its engagement with the local Lenape community.

KATONAH, NY — In 1680, English colonists bought the land that would become Bedford, New York, from a Munsee Lenape sachem named Katonah, meaning “great hill.” Today, his name belongs to a Westchester village that is now home to Branchline, the Gochman Family Collection’s (GFC) new gallery and studio space, which opened to the public on November 6 with Line Break, an exhibition of works drawn primarily from its holdings of contemporary Native American art.

Since its founding in 2021, GFC has collected over 800 works with support from Native and non-Native gallerists, artists, and curators alike, including Creative Director and Curator Rachel Martin (Tlingít), curator and Hyperallergic contributor Shándíín Brown (Diné), and Director Laura Phipps, who also serves as Branchline’s director. Designed by Elizabeth Roberts Architects, the new space occupies two historic storefronts steps from Katonah’s Metro-North station, with free-admission galleries, skylit artist studios, a community ceramics studio, and apartments for invited artists.

Branchline makes a public home for what has essentially been a lending operation: According to GFC, more than 260 of its works have appeared in over 100 exhibitions at institutions including the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Whitney Museum of American Art, and The Broad, and it charges no loan fees. That model speaks to a known problem with private collecting, explained Joseph Pierce (Cherokee), professor and founding director of the Native American and Indigenous Studies Initiative at Stony Brook University. “Just because you collect something doesn’t mean you’re going to show it,” Pierce told Hyperallergic. “The risk is that it doesn’t circulate.”

#9129. Brokies, This Met Gala Is for You

T-shirts revolutionize the Costume Institute’s programming, the sociability of MoMA’s Brancusi exhibit, and the curators of the 2028 Whitney Biennial announced.

A saturated blue sky and cascades of complementary golden-yellow foliage laid the foundation for a vibrant, picturesque Diwali weekend in the suburbs. It wasn’t the most festive Diwali for me — instead of lighting diyas and playing with sparklers, I spent a majority of the weekend hand-feeding a friendly yard squirrel while wearing some bullshit pajamas extracted from the depths of my childhood closet.

Think I’m slumming it? Well, think again! Because those dilapidated pajamas are almost certainly what inspired the theme for next year’s Met Gala and related Costume Institute exhibit: extraOrdinary: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday, a program “devoted to the undersung beauty and allure of quotidian garments.” (That’s code for jeans.)

(And t-shirts. And raincoats. Maybe pajamas, but also maybe not.)

It’s an exasperated, last-minute pivot after controversial British fashion designer John Galliano, who was central to the Costume Institute’s original program for 2027, withdrew from participating entirely this August in response to the public backlash toward his racist behavior in the past. Between “elevating” daily wear into runway fashion and exploring how “humble, even ‘disposable’ materials” like paper and aluminum can become wearable, this enormous exercise in putting a positive spin on gentrifying economic recession is at odds with NYC residents who are buckling from profound unaffordability as the city speedruns its transformation into a private equity playground.

I guess I can’t really say which is worse — the current standard of celebrities in bespoke, extravagant garments from elite fashion houses hanging off their GLP-1 frames, or the notion that a Met Gala dress code calling for aluminum foil pants, a shrunken tee, and maybe a jacket made from hole-punched plastic circles is what’ll push people to consider everyday wear in a different light.

However, before we get too pressed, we have to acknowledge that this is a big moment for the Bad Bunny x Zara collection! On the plus side, it might make it easier for some ~lowly civs~ to sneak in and eat all the cheese cubes. Dress for the job you want, right?

Speaking of jobs — Whitney Museum curator Meg Onli returns as a co-curator for the 2028 Whitney Biennial, sharing the stage with director and dancer Zack Winokur, who co-founded the interdisciplinary American Modern Opera Company in 2017. I found the 2026 Biennial to be a textbook case of the whole being less than the sum of its parts. Let’s see how Winokur’s hand in artistic performance direction manifests in this curatorial behemoth; I’m sure he’s used to working with a lot of moving parts.

Back to the here and now, I’m long overdue for multiple museum visits at the peak of the season. The days keep slipping through my fingers before I’ve had a chance to visit the Krasner Pollock show at The Met or the Architects of Liberation at the MoMA. Mayor Mamdani actually paid a visit to the MoMA show before I did, and he’s significantly busier than I am, so there’s really no excuse!

In another nudge for me to make the journey uptown, MoMA recently opened its Brancusi exhibition. With a replica of Brancusi’s studio and a selection of rare media documenting his work environment and the social atmosphere he cultivated between his sculptures and his guests alike, the exhibition spotlights the artist’s labor-intensive process as an art form in itself.

Critic Aruna D’Souza noted that the “sculptures seem to be maintaining COVID-era social distancing protocols,” and chalked that awkward dynamic up to the MoMA’s renovated gallery layout, recalling the previously approachable setup’s capacity to “allow for art objects to talk to each other.”

On Sunday, I bore witness to a conversation that made me think about Brancusi’s glinting buffed bronzes and smooth marbles. The chatter between a yellowing tree branch, an overturned recycling bin, and the white picket fence behind them might have been too maximalist compared to the Romanian sculptor’s sleek, pared-down modernism. Nevertheless, I pulled over to eavesdrop.

Among the historic wave of triumphs for Democrats in yesterday’s midterms, New York State Assemblywoman Claire Valdez, an artist, former cultural worker, and union organizer, was elected to represent New York’s 7th Congressional District in the United States House of Representatives. | Anna Lee

Having co-curated the 2024 Biennial, Onli returns to the next edition with Winokur, who founded the American Modern Opera Company. | Anna Lee

The artist’s work is glorious and resonant, but the Museum of Modern Art has a space problem, or an elegance problem, or a crowd mitigation problem. | Aruna D’Souza

A little more legibility would’ve benefited Alison Nguyen’s fragmented short film about the famed NYC artists’ housing complex. | Rhea Nayyar

For fans of the tiny tablet, this is a worthy upgrade.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For what feels like the first time in years, Apple is in experimenting mode. From folding iPhones to touchscreen MacBooks, the company is suddenly dropping innovative products rather than incremental upgrades. But while the new iPad mini might not be the most exciting new release of 2026, for a select group of users, it might just be the best iPad yet.

The 8th generation iPad mini upgrades almost everything about the tiny tablet. The headline feature has to be the OLED display, which is brighter, crisper and more vibrant than any iPad mini display we've seen. Meanwhile, minor design changes have resulted in a thinner and lighter body – which is a much more meaningful change than it might sound.

I've always been a fan of the iPad mini. Sure, larger models like the Pro feature M-series chips and ProMotion displays, but sometimes there's no replacement for portability. As the famous saying goes, 'your best iPad is the one you have with you' – and being able to sling the iPad mini into a tote bag is invaluable. And the first thing I noticed when picking it up was the reduction in size. At 5.4mm thick and 255 grams, it's just ridiculously thin and light.

And the second thing I noticed was, yes, that OLED display. While it isn't quite as stunning as the new MacBook Pro's PROLED XDR display, those bright colours and inky blacks look stunning. For creatives, a bright, colour-accurate screen is a must, and now the smallest iPad delivers one in spades.

But there is a glaring omission. In this day and age, a 60hz refresh rate feels slow and stuttering on any device, let alone one that starts at £699. Apple's 120hz ProMotion display has made its way to most of its products by now, but it's surprising, given the scale of the rest of the updates (and the price increase) that the iPad mini hasn't been blessed with one. Reddit, as you might imagine, has not been kind.

But if you can put aside the lack of ProMotion, there's so much to love here. Performance-wise, that A20 Pro chip (which also resides in the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo) is incredibly speedy and efficient – I'm managing to eke out around ten hours on a single charge.

Another improvement is the sound quality. Apple has somehow managed to place the speakers underneath the display (or as Apple calls it, the 'acoustic display'), and the result is powerfully punchy audio for a tablet so small.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Overall, if you're somebody who already loves the iPad mini and has the cash to burn for an upgrade, the 8th generation model is a winner. Every improvement adds up to a meaningfully enhanced experience, particularly the OLED screen and the weight loss. Now, if Apple could just bring itself to give us a 120hz display, the 9th generation iPad mini might just be the perfect tiny tablet.

#9127. Shanghai next? City’s art scene leans into an uncertain future

Since 2014, West Bund Art & Design (shown in 2025) has expanded to include multiple venues Courtesy West Bund Art & Design

Shanghai is a restless city. Its impatient hustle may spare its art scene from the plateau of middle age as it navigates a crisis of transition after the Covid years derailed its late 2010s momentum. Going into Shanghai’s annual art week (10-15 November), with two established fairs anchoring an explosion of art events across the city, its galleries, artists and institutions are assessing how the city’s art market can weather China’s economic slowdown and whether the cultural momentum of the past three decades can be sustained.

“Shanghai has so many galleries, so many museums, so many eccentric little spaces that you could come in the middle of summer and still see art non-stop,” says Lorenz Helbling, who founded ShanghArt in 1996. One of the first contemporary art galleries in China, it now has locations in Shanghai, Beijing and Singapore. The Swiss transplant says the volume of artistic activity in the city of 25 million people can be compared to New York’s, though the scene can be harder to find. “You can make a lot of fun things here.”

The city’s two large-scale fairs, Art021 Shanghai (11-14 November) and West Bund Art & Design (10-15 November), established in 2013 and 2014 respectively, set the barometer and prime the mood. So far, Shanghai’s core galleries have largely survived China’s property crash and deflationary economy, but they need young artists and new collectors to continue buoying their businesses.

Lise Li, who founded Shanghai’s Vanguard Gallery in 2004, says the city is “still in an upward phase, just growing much more slowly than before”. During art week, Li’s gallery will participate in the second iteration of the boutique fair Hangover Shanghai (11-15 November) and in Art021, while showing the artist Tang Chao in the gallery and collaborating on a group show at the artist-run 33ml Offspace. Several artists represented by Vanguard are having big moments nearby: Liao Fei will simultaneously be showing at Hangzhou’s Imagokinetics and the artist group known as Jiū Society has an exhibition at Nanjing’s Beiqiu Museum of Contemporary Art.

Established in 2013, Art021 Shanghai (pictured in 2025) is one of the most successful art fairs in the city Photo: Lisa Movius

Though the buzz of the 2010s has quieted, Li says, “there are quite a few more art institutions, and more newcomers are getting involved. The number of young artists is increasing rapidly; we see a lot of new faces every year. But most exhibitions are relatively conservative, which is rather a pity.”

The market has “changed considerably” compared to what now “might be called the ‘golden 15 years’ of China’s contemporary art market: the shift in the broader economic environment over the past few years has been impossible to ignore”, Otto Neu says. In 2022 he co-founded Nan Ke Gallery, which has a group show about art and literature on view during the fair week. “For artists and galleries alike, it is certainly a challenging moment. We probably have to work twice as hard as we did before simply to survive and keep things moving.”

Change, Neu adds, does not have to be negative. He cites the Chinese expression “great waves wash away the sand and leave the gold behind”, adding that “difficult periods can force an industry to become more focused, more rigorous and perhaps more honest about what really matters. In that sense, this may also be an important stage of maturation for Shanghai’s art scene.”

In addition to this month’s two international art fairs, Shanghai’s many resident artists—ranging from established figures like Ding Yi, Zhang Enli and Yang Fudong to mid-career and emerging talents—can rely on year-round programming at a healthy variety of homegrown and imported galleries. Western outfits like Almine Rech, Perrotin and Lisson maintain spaces in Shanghai, as do Asian powerhouses including Japan’s Ota Fine Arts and Korea’s Arario Gallery. ShanghArt has been joined by several influential local galleries, among them Antenna Space, Gallery Vacancy, Capsule Gallery and Don Gallery.

Major state-backed museums like the Power Station of Art, Museum of Art Pudong and West Bund Museum (which is partnered with the Centre Pompidou in Paris) have a complement of private museums that have proliferated since the 2010s. The Rockbund Art Museum, Long Museum and Yuz Museum are the best known, but smaller, newer, specialised or further-flung institutions like Fotografiska and the Museum of Glass, and non-profit spaces like Pond Society, Longlati and Prada Rong Zhai, have also enriched the Shanghai art ecosystem.

Vanguard Gallery’s Li credits Shanghai’s “open-city vibe” and its large base of collectors and visitors, along with the museums, galleries and artists, plus a citizenry curious “about fashion and new things, a strong history of business, and a diverse cultural structure. The main downside is that the cost of living is too high.” The lack of art information platforms, even in Chinese, is the other main challenge, she says.

The sense of openness is what drew the collector Cherry Xu to open her art-meets-fashion space Cheruby in the city last year. With new initiatives, “the boundaries between artists, designers, musicians and people working in fashion are becoming increasingly blurred”, she says, opening the art world to new audiences. “This kind of natural crossover between different fields is something very particular to Shanghai,” Xu says. “Art here doesn’t operate as an isolated system; it is constantly in conversation with design, music, fashion, technology and a broader youth culture, with these different communities influencing one another.”

Compared to Beijing’s art scene, Neu says, Shanghai’s creative community maintains a “healthy sense of distance. There is a certain independence between galleries, institutions, artists and collectors, which has shaped a rather distinctive ecosystem here”, a happy, pragmatic chaos of sorts. Beijing’s art scene is built on personal connections, Neu says, while in Shanghai, “between institutions, between galleries and even between galleries and collectors, there is often an understanding that business is business, friendship is friendship, and collaboration does not necessarily require complicated personal obligations or relationships”.

However, Neu adds that those divisions could become vulnerabilities in the current economic upheaval. “Perhaps this is precisely the moment when Shanghai’s art community needs to become a little more connected and cohesive than it has been in the past—not by giving up its independence, but by finding better ways to support one another,” he says.

Helbling says that Beijing is “more split up into scenes which work on their own”, while Shanghai has various circles that interact and are more permeable. He likens the city’s art community to its fairly compact geography, with the art neighbourhoods all within comparably easy reach of each other.

Twenty years ago, Shanghai was the upstart artistic challenger to Beijing, the political capital home to China’s leading art academy. Hong Kong’s concurrent cultural rise proved complimentary to Shanghai’s, and many in Shanghai say the expanding art activity in Korea, Japan and Singapore—as well as in mainland Chinese cities like Chengdu, Shenzhen and nearby Nanjing, Hangzhou and Suzhou—have been net positives for the local scene.

“This situation didn’t happen overnight; it’s the result of years of collaboration between Shanghai’s art institutions, galleries and fairs, as well as the collectors and artists living here,” Li says. “It’s not simply due to fairs or art weeks alone. The rise of art in new Chinese cities has also become developed, likely influenced by Shanghai and Hong Kong.”

Shanghai “was one of the earliest cities in China to develop a contemporary art market, and its relatively open culture and international outlook have given it a particular advantage”, Neu says. “Whether we are talking about collecting, aesthetic awareness or public understanding of contemporary art, Shanghai has accumulated more than two decades of experience and audience development. That kind of cultural infrastructure takes time to build.”

He adds that growing art scenes in other mainland cities represent “something very positive for Shanghai rather than a threat. A stronger regional art ecosystem ultimately creates more audiences, more conversations and more opportunities for everyone. Healthy competition and exchange between cities can only make the broader Chinese art scene more dynamic.”

Regionally, Xu says, Shanghai “has a very distinct local culture, its own audiences and creative communities, [while] its relationship with other Asian cities is becoming much more direct. It feels increasingly natural for artists, curators and other creative practitioners to live and work across different cities in Asia, and for us to look to what is happening in Tokyo, Seoul, Hong Kong, Singapore, Bangkok and elsewhere in the region, rather than instinctively treating Europe and the US as the only points of reference.” For Shanghai’s art week, Cheruby is showing a solo exhibition by the multidisciplinary Thai artist Tanat Teeradakorn.

“Shanghai has an interesting place within this network,” Xu says. “It has a relatively mature art infrastructure, but also very strong fashion, design, commercial, technological and popular cultures, and these worlds exist very close to one another in everyday life. It also has a large and increasingly young audience, so when an artist comes to Shanghai, they are encountering more than an established ‘art world’; they are entering a complex and fast-moving urban environment that is constantly being reshaped by new forms of consumption, technology and youth culture. That complexity creates a lot of possibilities.”

Zhang Ruyi, whose 2022 exhibition at Beijing’s UCCA Center for Contemporary Art is shown here, is among Shanghai’s mid-career artists to watch Photo: Sun Shi; courtesy UCCA Center for Contemporary Art

After helping to build the careers of some of Asia’s biggest art stars, Helbling now focuses on cultivating rising talents through more group shows and dialogue. “You always look at what artists are doing,” he says. “Many of them now operate between here and the West—educated here and in the West”, with networks and roots in both cultures.

After suspended mobility during the Covid years, dual-culture artists in Shanghai and across Asia have resumed their frequent travels between regions. Often the children of artists or collectors, young Chinese artists are very well versed in both Western and Asian artistic traditions, giving them a sophisticated perspective. “They have an interesting job to do to figure out what kind of art makes sense today,” Helbling says.

He recalls the “loneliness” of Shanghai’s 1990s avant-garde, now rendered “impossible” by contemporary art’s citywide popularity. Still, he views the 2000 internationalisation of the Shanghai Biennale, the first contemporary art fair SH Contemporary (2007-14), and the flowering of galleries and museums as all part of one era.

“There was from the 1990s when Shanghai opened up until the Covid time, and there is after Covid time,” he says. “The first 30 years, and now the second 30 years.”

#9126. Lagoons will weave through new Egyptian city masterplanned by SOM

International architecture studio SOM has unveiled plans for a new city in Egypt named Alam Al Roum, which will stretch 7.2 kilometres along the Mediterranean coastline.

Set to be built near Marsa Matrouh, the 20.6-square-kilometre masterplan features swimmable lagoons alongside 22 kilometres of seawater-connected lagoons, which will weave through the built environment to support stormwater management.

“The Mediterranean is home to some of the world’s great cities, shaped over centuries by climate, culture and economic forces,” said SOM principal Thomas Hussey.

“Alam Al Roum presents a rare opportunity to imagine a new city from the ground up, one that responds to the realities of climate change while offering an exceptional quality of life.”

SOM designed the masterplan around Egypt’s north coast landscape and climate, orienting buildings and public spaces to take advantage of coastal breezes and sunlight.

The development will be elevated to accommodate changing coastal conditions, while waterfront areas will be protected with natural interventions such as riparian buffers, stormwater wetlands, stabilised dunes and living shorelines.

Designed for developer Qatari Diar, Alam Al Roum will comprise beachfront and lagoon-side neighbourhoods, town centres, areas for hospitality and resorts, golfing facilities, an education district and a business hub.

A grand boulevard will form an urban spine connecting an international marina on the Mediterranean Sea with a mobility hub further inland.

Aiming to establish the city as a year-round cultural destination, Alam Al Roum’s waterfront downtown will contain a cultural pier, lighthouse, amphitheatre, yacht club, mosque, and markets.

The first phase of the city development is expected to commence in 2030, comprising a four-square-kilometre area with a beachfront stretch, open-sea-connected lagoons and a town-centre marina.

“Alam Al Roum represents our vision for a new generation of Mediterranean destinations – one that goes beyond the traditional seasonal resort to create a vibrant, year-round coastal city,” said Qatari Diar CEO Hamad bin Talal Al-Thani.

“We are bringing together nature, the sea, hospitality and everyday life within a carefully planned environment that reflects the unique character of Egypt’s north coast,” he continued.

“Through our partnership with SOM and our global network of experts, we are creating a destination that is rooted in its landscape and climate, while setting a new benchmark for integrated coastal development in the Mediterranean.”

In recent years, Egypt established a new capital city east of Cairo. The initial design concept for the city was designed by SOM and further developed by the international building consultancy Dar al-Handasah Shair & Partners.

KIFF's redesigned logo feels fresh and alive.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Film festivals don't have a direct impact on most people's lives. Few of us actually get around to attending one, and the films they feature rarely reach our nearest arts cinema, let alone the local multiplex. Yet, whether we ever buy a ticket to one, film festivals really do matter.

This is where new talent, both in front of and behind the camera, gets to show people what they're made of; where fresh and off-the-wall ideas get their first airing in public. A typical festival is a bubbling cauldron of visual styles, storytelling techniques and new voices, which will then gradually filter into mainstream cinema, advertising, music videos and more.

Occasionally too, a festival hit will break out in its own right. Reservoir Dogs started its journey at Sundance; Parasite at Cannes. Even if you've seen neither film, you'll have felt their ripple effects on culture in general.

Wth all that heated experimentation and ambition, you'd think a film festival logo would be another canvas for creativity. But too often, these events seem to just throw together a bunch of elements (a camera, a film reel, a clapperboard) without much thought. So it was a pleasant surprise to see the logo for the Kolkata International Film Festival (KIFF) does something very different.

Kolkata, formerly known as Calcutta, is the capital of West Bengal in India. This year the 32nd edition of its annual film festival runs from 16 to 23 December. Recently, its organisers revealed this new logo (shown above), which is the work of Sandip Ray.

Sandip is not only a filmmaker himself, he's also the son of the legendary Satyajit Ray: a director who was also a designer working on book covers, film posters and typefaces. And in this logo, Sandip has done his father proud.

Where the typical film festival logo juggles several references, this one commits to a single idea, and is all the better for it. Heavy black letters are cut into by burnt-orange triangles, each edged with sprocket holes like a strip of film.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

If someone had described that to me before I'd seen it, I'd probably have thought "That sounds awful". Film strips are the clip art of cinema: as big a cliché as a popcorn box, and increasingly anachronistic to boot.

But here, the execution is everything. Crucially, Sandip hasn't used the film strips as decoration of the logo, but as its foundation. They're not just a way of adding interest to the logo design; they are the logo design. It's the difference between committing to an idea and not actually having one in the first place.

To my mind, the triangles could be seen as doubling up as play and rewind buttons… although admittedly this might just be me.

Overall, the important thing about this logo is that it doesn’t look like anything else. I've spent so many years looking at perfectly formed sans serifs that it's made me weary. And the idea that more and more people are going to use AI tools that serve up an average of this style depresses me even more.

KIFF’s logo, in contrast, is chunky, angular and a bit odd. Some people might dislike it for that very reason. But I love the fact that two colours and one bold idea are all it needs to be instantly recognisable, and that’s got to be an inspiration for logo designers everywhere.

He is the author of the books The 50 Greatest Designers (Arcturus) and Great TED Talks: Creativity (Pavilion). What did those poor kids do to offend HBO's graphic designers?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In case you hadn't heard, there's a new Harry Potter series on the horizon. This December we're all hopping back on board the Hogwarts Express, only this time it's on TV, with HBO planning to serialise the entire book series over the next few years. The trailers so far have drawn sharp scrutiny – which you might expect, given the popularity of the films. And now, a new series of character posters is raising eyebrows.

What did those poor kids do to upset the editor of these posters? The designs each feature one of the principal cast members' faces in close-up, with their wand held aloft in front of it. Their faces are effectively cut in half by the wand, and some feel they look bizarrely stretched. Poor Ron seems to have been particularly afflicted. Not only that, but each half of the faces appears to be lit by a different light source, making the whole thing look weirdly spliced together. Suffice to say, these aren't among the best print ads we've seen.

New posters for HBO’s ‘HARRY POTTER’ series. Premieres December 25 on HBO. https://t.co/T8xqd9MCNDNovember 9, 2026

"Unfortunately, this is the first major mistake since the beginning of the marketing campaign. It’s already receiving a lot of negative reviews on the official pages. I’m shocked they released it like this, especially after how flawless the attention to detail has been from the very beginning," one Redditor comments. Another adds, "Each poster looks like they took one half of their face from two different photos and combined them along their wands. Absolute terrible editing work, imo."

And to add insult to injury, fans have quickly knocked together an improved take on the design, focussing on just one half of each characters' face. These are arguably more striking and dramatic, and, more importantly, the faces don't look distractingly wide.

Time will tell whether the series lives up to the books, or the original film series. But one thing's for sure: these aren't among the best posters of the year, let alone all time.

#9123. Peruvian senator calls for removal of large-scale replicas of Moche erotic sculptures from public park

One of the huaco erótico sculptures in Fertility Park, near Trujillo, Peru Photo: Richard Avila, via Wikimedia Commons

A controversy over 3m-tall erotic sculptures in northern Peru reignited recently after a senator requested that the cultural ministry remove them from a public area. Located in a park outside the city of Trujillo, the sculptures are replicas of ceramics from the pre-Incan Moche civilisation.

“What happens when children see these images? Neurological and psychological factors are affected, because they see body dimensions that are completely different from how they see themselves,” Milagros Jáuregui, a conservative senator from the Renovación Popular party, said in a speech on 26 October.

The sculptures are located in Parque de la Fertilidad (Fertility Park), a public space where in 2021 then-mayor Arturo Fernández of the Moche district began installing giant fibreglass reproductions of ceramic depictions of sexual acts to promote tourism.

Known as huacos eróticos, the much smaller original ceramics date from the 3rd to 8th century AD. No more than 30cm in height, they were placed in tombs as burial offerings. But the debate about their much larger versions in the park goes beyond political prudishness.

“It’s a complicated issue,” the Peruvian archaeologist Walter Alva tells The Art Newspaper. “There’s freedom to express or re-create themes from the past, but these ceramics were created to be placed as offerings to the dead, with a sense of revitalising life. They are associated with both fertility and an entire system of beliefs.”

An original huaco erótico ceramic offering made by the Moche civilisation, Larco Museum, Lima Photo: László Varga, via Wikimedia Commons

The Moche civilisation covered 700km of the coast of what is now Peru, between the regions of Piura and Ancash, centuries before the Inca dominated the area. “Moche art is primarily ceramic, and these vessels depict erotic scenes or concepts of sexuality from that era,” Alva says. “The sculptures in the park were created outside of their historical context.”

One of the greatest archaeological discoveries from the Moche civilisation was that of the Lord of Sipán near the city of Chiclayo—a discovery Alva made in 1987. A 3rd-century monarch, the Lord of Sipán’s body was found covered with gold along with eight other people, a dog and two llamas and nearly 500 objects including ceramic vessels, ornaments and textiles.

The Moche have the largest number of erotic representations among pre-Hispanic civilisations. The most complete collection of its ceramics is in Lima, at the Larco Museum of pre-Columbian art, which celebrated its centennial in July. Before the 1960s, children were forbidden from entering the room that housed the huacos. Today, minors must be accompanied by an adult. The institution’s Erotic Gallery is one of its most popular attractions.

Jáuregui, an evangelical pastor as well as a senator, believes these Moche sculptures should only be in closed spaces. “Displaying these types of images in public is harmful to children,” she told congress. “We should have them in museums, where high-school students can observe a part of our culture that is a national treasure with the help of teachers or some kind of tutor.”

The well-preserved statue is one of the oldest artefacts discovered in the Chan Chan archaeological site

Excavations at the Cerro Mayal site in the north of the country show it was an important production facility for Moche ceramics around the seventh century

#9122. Linehouse reimagines industrial aesthetics for Jen Hangzhou hotel in Kohn Pedersen Fox-designed building

Photography by Jonathan Leijonhufvud and Wen Studio

International studio Linehouse has completed the interiors of the Jen hotel in Hangzhou, China, which features details that nod to local craft and the area’s industrial heritage.

The hotel, which is owned by the Shangri-La Hotel Group, is located along Hangzhou’s Dongxin River in an urban setting and flanked by two former industrial factory compounds.

The 18-floor hotel building was designed by US architecture firm Kohn Pedersen Fox, using steel, grey brick and glass to reference the site’s industrial past.

The same design approach was extended into the interior by Linehouse, which focuses on showcasing local craft and nods to the industrial elements of the former factories.

“Jen Hangzhou is an urban hotel that celebrates its neighbourhood context – one that layers history, craft, culture and rich materiality into a new perspective on Hangzhou,” Linehouse said.

The studio used earth-toned marble, oak panelling and relaxed furniture in the ground-floor lobby to create a calm and warm atmosphere.

At the entrance, guests are greeted by a textured artwork by artist Elsa Jeandedieu that depicts an abstract version of the bridges and canal close to the hotel.

Patchwork patterns on the marble floor and on a bespoke rug in the lobby were informed by the street layout and tile patterns of the surrounding neighbourhood.

All the hospitality spaces, including a restaurant, a bar and function rooms are located on the sixth floor.

The long, linear OpenHouse restaurant is wrapped by full-height glazing that invites natural light inside.

A timber design feature spans the ceiling and was informed by the craft of sunmao, a traditional timber joinery technique. It is highlighted by a thin black metal frame that supports suspended lighting.

At the centre of the restaurant, a coffee bar splits the space into a dining area on one side and an all-day lounge on the other.

In the private dining room, the timber canopy has an angled design and is decorated with burnt red and yellow hues. In the rest of the OpenHouse restaurant, rooms feature teal tiles and handmade ceramic wall lighting.

The adjacent Koan Bar is a triple-height venue characterised by an undulating black metal staircase that takes guests to a terrace on the upper floor, with incorporated platforms where guests can socialise.

The sinuous staircase is carved between walls lined with concrete panels, another nod to the site’s industrial heritage.

Beneath it, curved booths in walnut timber and tan leather provide intimate seating spaces.

Three interconnected spaces on the sixth floor, enveloped by undulating timber walls, will be used for events and intimate social gatherings. Like in the lobby, bespoke carpets feature patterns abstracted from urban details in the neighbourhood.

The seventh floor is dedicated to wellness and comprises a gym, a yoga room, a spa, a pool and changing rooms, made from tactile materials with muted tones to create a calm environment.

At the gym, a lava stone wall has engravings that illustrate movement, while the yoga room features hand-chiseled timber panels.

A sloped skylit annex accommodates the swimming pool.

The 176 guest rooms were conceived as “urban retreats”. Here, Linehouse used a restrained palette of gun metal, oak datum, textured render and tan leather to underline the industrial aesthetic.

“The public areas explore traditional craft techniques such as sunmao timber joinery, clay tiling and bricks, natural patterns, textures and renders, whilst the guestrooms explore a refined industrial aesthetic,” Linehouse said.

“Red brick, concrete, metal and bold forms reference the surrounding industrial environment whilst handcrafted tiles, vintage timber, colours and metals with different patinas introduce warmth, richness and texture.”

The guest rooms have curved ceilings that create indirect lighting and add softness to the space, while the bathrooms are illuminated by glass-block walls.

Founded by Alex Mok and Briar Hickling in 2013, Linehouse is an architecture and interior practice with studios in Shanghai, Hong Kong and Auckland.

It has recently designed Ink Ink Market in Shanghai with a translucent sloping facade, as well as the interiors for Bangkok’s Central Park shopping centre with three dramatic atriums, which was shortlisted of Retail Interior (large) by this year’s Dezeen Awards.

Area: 12,850 sqm Client: Kerry Properties Operator: Shangri-La Design principal: Alex Mok Design team: Wang Jue, Jingru Tong, Yunbin Lou, Cherngyu Chen, Inez Low, Yeling Guo, Aiwen Shao, Mia Zhou, Norman Wang, Yuechen Wu Lighting: LPA Decorative lighting: Kris Lite, Van Collection, Yi Design, Yun Zhao Studio, Fine Lumens, Santa & Cole, Audo, Timothy Oulton, La Nuit Design consultant: EDGE Design Interior contractor: Terart Decoration Design & Engineering Co., Ltd, Shenzhen Lead management consultant: Wong & Ouyang (HK) Ltd. #9121. Contemporary Stained-Glass Windows Installed in Notre-Dame, Spanish Man Awarded $1.12 M. for Renaissance Door Discovery, and More: Morning Links for November 10, 2026

To receive Morning Links in your inbox every weekday, sign up for our Breakfast with ARTnews newsletter.

WINDOW OF OPPORTUNITY. New stained-glass windows by French artist Claire Tabouret have been quietly installed in the Notre-Dame de Paris cathedral and will be unveiled to the public on December 7, reports Le Figaro. The project, backed by French President Emmanuel Macron, has faced controversy, but has moved forward against all odds, overcoming one legal challenge while still facing another. The six new windows feature a color-rich, figurative telling of the story of the Pentecost and have been placed along the nave’s southern aisle. The windows were made with the Simon-Marq workshop in Reims and for now, they are reportedly hidden behind red curtains. Meanwhile, heritage groups have opposed the project because it requires the removal of existing 19th-century stained-glass windows designed by Eugène-Emmanuel Viollet-le-Duc, who intended them as part of a cohesive homage to Gothic architecture. BRINGING HOME THE CANADIAN BACON. Things are looking up for Canadian artists who are still grappling with US tariffs. The country has just proposed a federal budget that exempts artists from paying taxes on C$45,000 ($38,000) of their earnings, reports The Art Newspaper. “In Budget 2026, we’re backing the Canadian artists who tell our stories,” wrote Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in a November 5 social media post. “That means if you’re a Canadian artist, you won’t pay tax on up to C$45,000 of income derived from your creative work,” he added. And that’s not all; the proposed budget also pledges C$783.1 million ($554 million) over five years to the National Arts Centre, Library and Archives Canada, the National Battlefields Commission and national museums. Visitors under 25 will also get free entry to national museums, thanks to C$46.3 million ($32.8 million) in subsidies for the same five years, followed by C$11.5 million ($8.1 million) per year. Not to be forgotten, the Canada Council for the Arts will get C$20 million ($14.1 million) over three years. However, some tell TAN the funding is still short of what is needed. “As a sector, we still have a lot of questions, while many artists need relief now,” said Jenna Faye Powell, interim national executive director of Carfac (Canadian Artists’ Representation/Le Front des Artistes Canadiens).

The 4 a.m., August 28, 1963, handwritten final draft of Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr’s historic “I Have a Dream” speech is being offered for sale at Christie’s New York to benefit charity on January 22, 2027. [ArtDependence]

In an open letter appealing to the Nuremberg City Council, a contemporary arts association has warned of the possible closure of the 1967-founded Kunsthalle Nürnberg amid a strained public budget. [Monopol Magazine]

Artist Olafur Eliasson is partnering with ARoS Aarhus Art Museum in Denmark to create a publicly accessible study space and library containing research materials about Eliasson’s practice, opening alongside a major solo exhibition dedicated to him, plus newly installed artwork and more. [Ocula]

Artist Ryan Gander dishes on the YBA’s “egocentric, attention-seeking, shallow kind of art.” Plus, the act of drawing and painting being “futile and dumb,” despite including several of his own new paintings in his latest show, “Maybe: Ryan Gander” at Towner gallery in Eastbourne. [The Guardian]

WHEN ONE DOOR CLOSES … A decade after, Juan Francisco León Catena, a resident of Úbeda in southern Spain, chanced upon a magnificent Renaissance doorway hidden behind the walls of his property under renovation—he will be awarded a €1 million prize ($1.12 million) for his trouble, reports El País. Following a long legal battle, León Catena is poised to receive the award, granted by the Spanish Historical Heritage Law for chance, significant artistic finds. In this case, that find is a 15th-century portal from a former hospital church designed by Spanish Renaissance architect Andrés de Vandelvira. Discovered in excellent condition, experts deemed it of “great aesthetic value” and a unique Renaissance artwork. However, the local Andalusian Regional Government initially refused to pay up in a case that made its way to the High Court of Justice of Andalusia, which ultimately rejected their arguments. Now, León Catena is in talks with the city of Úbeda on how to best promote the heritage site, and there is the additional question of surrounding, city-owned buildings that also house the relic but are in dire need of restoration and risk collapse.

How much control you keep is the big question as Adobe goes all in on AI ahead of Adobe Max.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Adobe has spent the past couple of years trying to convince us that generative AI belongs in the creative process, and at Adobe Max in Miami this week, it’s going all in. Here’s the thing: Firefly is no longer a text-to-image toybox for mum’s designing birthday invites. It’s being rebuilt as a proper, all-encompassing AI creative studio that pulls Adobe’s own tools, a stack of third-party AI models and a new Creative Agent into one place, and Adobe’s pitch is simple: if you bring the vision and judgement, its AI sidekick, the agent, will do the legwork.

Rather than prompting a model for one AI-made image, you describe what you want in plain language, and the new Agent orchestrates Adobe’s tools and a growing list of AI models to get there. You stay in the director’s chair, with the option to review the agent’s plan before it starts, pick a model yourself or leave it on auto-select, and step in whenever you like. Adobe believes this workflow will bring new projects within reach that were once out of reach and builds on Firefly and other Adobe AI tools added to Photoshop, Illustrator and Premiere Pro over the last three years.

It's a similar Agentic approach we learned about when Nvidia announced its plans for NVIDIA RTX Spark, to connect 3D apps in one AI-controlled space.

Firefly Design, in beta, is a new editor built from scratch, with vector, image editing, animation, 3D and print on one collaborative canvas. You can work with AI, use Adobe’s precision tools, or move between the two. The image editor gets new tools for objects, text and lighting, including Edit Object, Edit Text, Relight and Retouch, plus a gallery of dozens of Quick Actions for small jobs like removing an object or knocking out a thumbnail.

In a demo ahead of Adobe Max, I learned how it all links up. A Firefly Boards project, with fonts from Adobe Fonts’ library of around 35,000 typefaces, carried straight into the Firefly Video Editor. Adobe Stock supplied the music, ElevenLabs the text-to-speech, and the new cut detection did in seconds what Adobe’s own presenter says can take minutes, even hours. Title motion presets are in there too.

Firefly also offers models from Google, Kling, OpenAI, ByteDance and ElevenLabs alongside Adobe’s own and Topaz Labs’, with recent additions including Kling 4.0 and Dreamina Seedance 2.5. If you already pay for several of these services, seeing them under one roof will appeal. But this also raises more questions about Adobe’s famously ethical AI approach, as the foxes are now in the henhouse. I’ll be interested to see how this plays out.

Back to the details, Firefly Graph is in beta and lets you string tools and models together, save the result and run it again whenever you need to. Builder is still in private beta; you type a prompt, and it spits out a clickable prototype for a site or app, and Adobe claims it won’t wander off your design system. That’s the claim I’d test first, because most AI prototyping tools drift the moment you ask for something unusual.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Adobe is also previewing ‘always-on agents’ (sounds ominous) that keep recurring work moving while you’re away, like organising assets and checking quality. For example, a restaurant owner gives an agent their menus, URL, and brand assets. The agent drafts weekly social posts for approval, learns from feedback, and reports back on performance.

The agent is also spreading beyond Firefly into Adobe’s flagship desktop apps, including Illustrator, Premiere, InDesign, After Effects, and Frame.io, though the AI Assistants there are still in beta (in Photoshop only, in the Photoshop beta app). What caught my eye is that Adobe is also opening the door to rivals. The local MCP integrations, previewed now and due in private beta in early 2027, will let you point your preferred third-party agent at native Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere and After Effects project files on your own computer. Layers, vectors, bins and sequences stay editable, so you can step in and fix things yourself. Plenty of pros already use outside agents, and Adobe clearly wants its apps to do their work where they do it.

Away from the agent, the app updates keep coming. After Effects gets an AI assistant that can make sense of an inherited project, debug expressions and generate images and video. Photoshop gets Relight, Generative Restyle and Quick Compare, and its remove tool now spots associated elements such as shadows. Lightroom adds Glow, one-tap blemish removal and a beta Open Eyes fix for dodgy blinks. Separately, Topaz Labs, which Adobe recently acquired, has introduced two new models, Wonder 4 and Image HDR, for upscaling, denoising, deblurring, sharpening and HDR. Illustrator gets refreshed content libraries and new on-canvas Blend controls, and InDesign gets a co-editing beta, Flex Layout for text frames and rewrite tools.

The idea that the artist stays in charge is Adobe's way of easing bad news for any creative fearing how AI is affecting them, and I can believe that for filing, resizing, and checking. Whether that holds once the agent makes calls on composition, layout, and style is the big question, and the more capable these tools get, the blurrier that line will be.

Adobe still has to show that more automation really does mean more time spent making things, and that comes down to how much control creatives get once the demos are over. More importantly, with agentic AI now a trend and spreading to more and more creative software, artists and creatives who want to stay AI-free will find it harder than before.

Buy Now Pay Later services let you split a purchase into installments — typically four payments over six weeks (Afterpay, Klarna "Pay in 4") or monthly payments over 3-36 months (Affirm, Klarna financing). The checkout process is seamless: enter your name and email, get instantly approved, and walk away with your purchase having paid only the first installment.

BNPL providers make money in two ways. First, they charge merchants 4-8% of each transaction — significantly more than the 2-3% credit card processing fee. Merchants accept this because BNPL increases average order values by 30-50%. Second, some providers charge interest on longer-term plans, and nearly all charge late fees when you miss a payment.

The "interest-free" label on short-term plans deserves scrutiny. While you may not pay interest, the behavioral cost is substantial. Research from multiple financial studies shows that BNPL users spend 30-50% more per transaction than they would with cash or debit. The psychological separation of the purchase from the full payment removes the natural spending brake that keeps budgets in check.

The financial industry has known for decades that separating the moment of purchase from the moment of payment increases spending. Credit cards exploit this. BNPL takes it further by making the payment feel even smaller — "just four easy payments of $37.50" feels dramatically different from "$150" even though it is the same amount.

A 2026 survey found that 43% of BNPL users have missed at least one payment. Among those who missed payments, the average person missed three or more over the prior year. Late fees compound quickly — four missed $8 Afterpay fees on a $200 purchase adds $32, effectively creating a 16% surcharge on what was supposed to be interest-free.

The credit score impact is evolving rapidly. As recently as 2022, most BNPL activity was invisible to credit bureaus. That has changed. Affirm now reports all payment activity to Experian and TransUnion. Afterpay reports to Equifax. Klarna reports financing plans to all three bureaus. On-time BNPL payments may slightly help your score, but missed payments can drop it significantly — and the damage lasts up to seven years.

For anyone pursuing financial independence, BNPL represents the opposite of the FI mindset. FI is built on intentional spending, high savings rates, and letting compound growth work in your favor. BNPL encourages impulsive spending, fragments your cash flow, and creates obligations that reduce your ability to invest.

There is exactly one scenario where BNPL is financially rational: a planned, budgeted purchase at 0% interest where you would have paid the full price regardless. For example, you need a new dishwasher, you have the $800 in savings, and the retailer offers four interest-free payments. You keep your $800 invested for six more weeks while paying in installments. The benefit is tiny — a few dollars of investment returns — but the cost is genuinely zero if you make every payment on time.

Outside this narrow scenario, BNPL is almost always a worse choice than the alternatives.

The financial independence community is nearly unanimous: BNPL is a trap disguised as convenience. The entire BNPL business model depends on you spending more than you planned. If you were going to buy the item anyway and you have the cash, just buy it. If you do not have the cash, that is your budget telling you something important.

The question to ask before any BNPL checkout: "Would I buy this right now if I had to pay the full price in cash today?" If the answer is no, BNPL is not helping you afford something — it is helping you overspend. If the answer is yes, just pay cash and skip the installment tracking, the payment reminders, and the risk of a missed payment damaging your credit.

For those building toward financial independence, every dollar matters. The 30-50% spending increase that BNPL encourages directly reduces your savings rate — the single most important variable in determining how quickly you reach FI.

Mortgage lenders are increasingly scrutinizing BNPL obligations during the underwriting process. Multiple active BNPL plans — even if interest-free — show up as recurring liabilities and can affect your debt-to-income ratio. If you are planning to apply for a mortgage or auto loan in the next 6-12 months, pay off all BNPL balances and avoid opening new ones. Lenders view fragmented installment obligations as a sign of cash flow stress, even if you have never missed a payment.

Affirm is a legitimate, publicly traded company (AFRM on NASDAQ). It is safe in the sense that it will not steal your money or identity. However, being legitimate does not mean it is a good financial decision. Affirm's interest rates range from 0-36% APR depending on creditworthiness, and the company reports all payment activity to credit bureaus.

Increasingly, yes. Affirm reports to Experian and TransUnion. Afterpay reports to Equifax. Klarna financing plans report to all three bureaus. On-time payments may help slightly, but a single missed payment can significantly damage your score and remains on your report for up to seven years.

Afterpay charges an $8 late fee per missed payment, capped at 25% of the order value. After multiple missed payments, your account is suspended, the balance is sent to collections, and the delinquency is reported to Equifax. Collections accounts damage your credit score severely and remain for seven years.

Klarna's "Pay in 4" plan is interest-free with no late fees, but your account may be suspended for missed payments. Klarna's longer-term financing plans charge 7.99-33.99% APR, involve a hard credit pull, and report to all three credit bureaus. Read the terms carefully — the word "Klarna" covers very different products.

It is possible but unlikely for most people. Research consistently shows that BNPL increases spending by 30-50% per transaction. If you have the discipline to use BNPL only on planned, budgeted purchases at 0% interest — and never miss a payment — the financial harm is minimal. But for most users, the behavioral cost exceeds any convenience benefit.

Because it works — for the store. Merchants pay BNPL providers 4-8% of each transaction (vs 2-3% for credit cards) because BNPL increases average order values by 30-50% and reduces cart abandonment by 20-30%. The merchant is paying for you to spend more. That should tell you who this arrangement benefits.

Buy Now Pay Later is a marketing innovation designed to make you spend more — and the data confirms it works. BNPL users spend 30-50% more per transaction, 43% miss payments, and the credit reporting implications are growing. The only responsible use case is a planned, budgeted purchase at 0% interest where you already have the cash. For everyone else, especially those pursuing financial independence, BNPL is a detour in the wrong direction. Pay with cash, invest the difference, and let compound growth work for you instead of against you.

#9118. Julia Stoschek Collection to Celebrate 20 Years with ‘Selfish in Bed’ Exhibition and Düsseldorf Reopening

Sarah Lucas doesn’t appear particularly apologetic in her 2000 self-portrait Selfish in Bed II. Standing with her hands on her hips, the British artist wears a black T-shirt with the words “SELFISH IN BED” printed across the front. Next April, that cheeky photograph will set the tone for a major group exhibition celebrating the 20th anniversary of the Julia Stoschek Collection in Düsseldorf, Germany.

Aptly titled Selfish in Bed, the exhibition opens on April 10, 2027, and will bring together 52 works by 43 artists, including Tracey Emin, Bill Viola, Wolfgang Tillmans, and Bruce Nauman. Selfish in Bed marks the inaugural exhibition of the reopened Julia Stoschek Foundation’s Düsseldorf headquarters, which closed for renovations in April 2025. Related Articles Collectors Jill and Peter Kraus Want Artists to Look at Their Upstate New York Property and React to It A New Hudson Valley Art Space Promises to Be As Accessible as It Is In Flux

Curated by Krist Gruijthuijsen, the director of Finland’s EMMA – Espoo Museum of Modern Art and former director of Berlin’s KW Institute for Contemporary Art, the show looks at how we construct our identities, express our sexuality, and present ourselves to the world.

The exhibition takes the bed as its starting point. It’s a place increasingly of contradictions: It’s private and vulnerable, yet inter-connected, where we spend hours scrolling through the images and opinions that shape how we see ourselves. The show explores that tension through works spanning the late 1960s to the present, including several that the foundation has never exhibited before.

There are more than a few highlights. Emin’s Why I Never Became a Dancer (1995), Simon Fujiwara‘s Joanne (2016/2018), and Hannah Wilke’s Through the Large Glass (1976), all explore women’s relationships with their bodies, sexuality, and public image. Meanwhile Monica Bonvicini‘s Destroy She Said (1998) challenges traditional domestic roles, and Ed Atkins’s Us Dead Talk Love (2012) examines questions of identity and authenticity in the digital age.

The exhibition is set to span two floors, and include video projections, mirrored surfaces, glass walls, and television monitors creating an immersive environment. Works by Viola, Tillmans, and Rosemarie Trockel will be presented together in a grouping that explores the human experience from birth onward.

For Stoschek, whose collection now includes more than 1,000 works by over 300 artists, the anniversary is also an opportunity to reflect on two decades of collecting.

“I am a very emotional collector,” Stoschek said in a statement. “An artwork has to get under my skin. I need images that stay with me.”

The Düsseldorf headquarters, housed in a converted industrial building dating to 1907, has undergone an extensive renovation by Berlin architecture firm Kuehn Malvezzi, which originally adapted the space for exhibitions in 2007. In Berlin, the foundation closed its exhibition space at the end of October after a decade of programming, shifting its attention toward Düsseldorf and international projects.

A publication marking the collection’s 20th anniversary will accompany the exhibition, with contributions from writers and critics including Rachel Cusk, Chris Kraus, Dean Kissick, and McKenzie Wark.

Selfish in Bed will run from April 10 through December 19, 2027, with an opening reception on April 9.

#9117. Studio Shea designs South Carolina library as "community living room"

Photography by Keith Isaacs (unless stated otherwise)

Brooklyn-based practice Studio Shea has completed a metal-clad library with a central atrium that draws on the civic and industrial context of its site in South Carolina, USA.

Clinton Public Library serves a railroad junction town of less than 8,000 residents.

The 11,000-square-foot (1,021-square metre) library translates the vernacular porch feature as well as the town’s agricultural and textile manufacturing heritage into a contemporary public building, Justin Shea, founder of Studio Shea, told Dezeen.

“At its core, the project was conceived as a welcoming community living room,” Shea said.

Set on 1.25 acres, the building’s scale and massing respond to its surrounding residential context in view of the town’s downtown corridor.

“The deep roof overhang creates a shaded front porch that recalls the familiar social role of the porch as a place for gathering,” Shea said, explaining that the low-pitched roofs and striated standing-seam metal cladding are a subtle nod to the area’s material character.

“Together, these elements give the library a contemporary identity while maintaining a clear connection to the character and history of Clinton.”

Inside, the library centres around a daylit atrium that is both the social and organisational heart of the program spaces and collections.

From the entrance, library patrons can see through the atrium to the collections, study areas, activity spaces and reading garden in a clear, easy-to-navigate scheme.

“Particular attention was given to the quality of natural light,” said Shea.

“A continuous clerestory draws soft, even daylight deep into the building, activating the interior throughout the day. At night, the illuminated atrium reverses that relationship, allowing the library to glow outward as a beacon for the community.”

The plan was designed for adaptability and flexibility, with the makerspace, children’s room, and meeting areas expanding into the center for larger workshops and the community room connecting with the lobby, service spaces and exterior plaza for after-hours events.

Inside, pops of colour, monochromatic spaces and varied textures create a playful environment suited to a broad range of ages and activities, while generous glazing contributes to the sense of openness.

A key element of the design is a community bench along the building’s exterior – designed by Studio Shea and fabricated with oak trees from the site by Piedmont Technical College – that ties into the lobby bench, circulation desk and collection shelving.

“What might otherwise have been an incidental site resource became a tangible expression of local participation and investment,” Shea explained.

“Public architecture can create a stronger sense of ownership when the community is given opportunities to participate in its creation,” he continued.

“A civic building does not need to be monumental to be significant; it can achieve meaning through being welcoming, useful, adaptable and genuinely connected to the people and place it serves.”

Other public buildings recently completed in South Carolina include a county administration building with “crisp edges” by Foster + Partners, the International African American Museum that floats above water by Pei Cobb Freed & Partners and Moody Nolan and a seaside restaurant designed for nostalgia by SDCO and Basic Projects.

These machines offer new creative opportunities to designers, illustrators and crafters.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Until recently, if you wanted to print onto, say, a phone case, a slate coaster or a leather notebook cover, you'd have to either pay a print shop, or blow a fortune on an industrial flatbed. Now, magically, that's all changed.

A new wave of desktop UV printers has arrived at affordable prices and manageable sizes. And they offer exciting new creative opportunities to designers, illustrators, crafters and anyone wanting to make stuff to sell on Etsy.

A UV printer jets ink onto an object and cures it instantly with ultraviolet light, so the ink sits on top of the surface rather than soaking in. If you want, you can build it up in layers to create raised, tactile textures. Many of the best UV printers also add white ink for printing onto dark or clear materials, and a varnish channel for gloss and spot effects. Of course, there's also the old fashioned choice of the best 3D printers out there, but make no mistake – UV printers use use a far more sophisticated (and expensive) technology.

In the article below, I've listed the three best UV printers on the market today, along with two Kickstarter projects that are well worth keeping an eye on (and potentially supporting, if you believe in the project).

xTool is best known for making some of the best laser cutters, and the O1 Omni is its first UV printer, which it describes as a 4-in-1.

You can use it for UV printing onto standard surfaces. It can also make UV DTF transfer stickers for curved and awkward surfaces. And the top-of-the-range, "UV + DT" model can print directly onto cotton (DTG), and onto film for heat transfer to fabric (DTF). If you want to do all of those things, then, you're saving yourself from buying two or three separate machines.

It's also very precise. Rather than relying on a fixed overhead camera, which distorts things towards the edge of the frame, xTool's Pixel-Scan system combines laser sensing with a scanning imager to map the bed one-to-one.

On the downside, the O1 Omni prints a whole job at the height of the tallest object, so mixing a chunky item with flat coasters can leave the lower ones blurred. It's also big and heavy (41kg) so you'll need a sturdy surface to work from. On the plus side, xTool's cartridges are pretty affordable. And overall, if you want one machine that does nearly everything, this is the top dog.

Eufymake is a sub-brand of global hardware company Anker, and the E1 is arguably the machine that kicked off the desktop UV boom. It became the most-funded project in Kickstarter history, made TIME's list of Best Inventions of 2025, and is now on sale generally.

If you want something that's easy to set up and use, this is it. The UV printer arrives fully assembled, the cartridge system means you don't have to mess about with syringes or bottles, and it's quick and easy to get from unboxing to a first print. The E1 stacks ink up to 5mm high, allowing 3D texture effects. You can in theory, then, reproduce brushstrokes on a canvas print, raised lettering on a business card or a leathery grain on a phone case. There's an optional rotary attachment for printing on curved surfaces like mugs and tumblers.

It's not perfect: the cartridges are more expensive than rivals', so if you're printing at scale that's worth considering. On the plus side, it's around half the size and weight of the Xtool, making it easy to fit into a home studio. In short, this is the one we'd recommend if you're new to the world of UV printing.

Procolored has been making DTF and UV printers for small print businesses for years. Its UV printer, the Procolored V4, was created primarily for one specific job: printing onto phone cases.

The 120 x 170mm A5 bed with a 15mm height limit is the perfect size for a large smartphone case laid flat. An infrared sensor measures the height of what's on the bed, and you align your designs using printed guides. The V4 is able to print onto cases made of hard plastic, soft silicone and glass. It doesn't just work on phones, either: Other small, flat items such as acrylic keyrings, badges, tiles and metal nameplates work too, as long as they fit within the print area.

Ink comes from bottles not cartridges, which helps keep running costs affordable. The V4 automatically cleans its head every 10 hours when it's left on, using about 1ml of ink a day, to keep the nozzles from clogging.

On the downside, it's slower than the newer machines and there's no varnish channel for gloss or raised textures. The software only works on Windows, and isn't the simplest to use. And for only slightly more money, you can get one of the larger all-rounders above. If you only want to print on phone cases, though, the V4 delivers exactly what it promises.

These UV printers haven't actually shipped yet, so we haven't included them in our main list. They're close to doing so though, so assuming all goes well, they're well worth keeping an eye on.

Most desktop UV printers slide the bed back and forth under the printhead. On the Morpho UV Printer, the head moves on a gantry, allowing more space for taller objects: 168mm of clearance, to be specific. The bed will bear items up to 10kg, and Morpho is also promising G7-certified colour calibration for print-shop consistency. It looked pretty good to us at the consumer electronics show IFA this September: here's a short video of it making a bookmark for us.

We don't know much more at this stage, though. This is a crowdfunded product, with shipping estimated between December 2026 and January 2027. But hands-on reports have been positive, and if tall or heavy objects are your thing, it's worth watching closely.

Heygears has spent years making resin 3D printers for dental and audio manufacturing, and with the G1X, it's applying that expertise to UV printing. In its standard form it's a high-end desktop UV printer, but it's built to grow: the Full-3D Pack will add a resin system that lets the same machine build full-colour 3D objects layer by layer.

Even if you never touch the 3D side, though, it looks like a serious UV printer. It uses Epson's industrial i3200 head, which is rated for up to two years and is less prone to clogging, along with eight ink channels for a wider colour range. Again, this is a crowdfunded launch, with shipping targeted for December.

In general, the best UV printers can print on any rigid, flat surface: wood, acrylic, metal, glass, slate, leather, ceramic, plastic and canvas, along with ready-made blanks like phone cases, coasters, keyrings and notebook covers. However, there are exceptions. To print onto clothing, you'll need a machine with DTG or DTF capability, such as the Xtool O1 Omni UV + DT edition. Very smooth surfaces such as glass and metal may need a primer for the best adhesion. And you'll need a rotary attachment for mugs, tumblers and bottles.

Generally yes, as long as you use common sense. However, uncured UV ink can irritate skin, so wear gloves when changing ink or cleaning your printer, and keep it away from children and pets. The inks can also give off a smell, so use the printer in a well-ventilated room.

Ink is the main ongoing cost of running a UV printer, and prices vary widely between brands. So compare the cost per millilitre and check whether the printer uses its own cartridges or refillable bottles. The printhead is a consumable too: cheaper heads may need replacing every six to 12 months. It's worth noting that UV printers need regular use, as ink that's left sitting around for too long can clog the head.
