#9114. Only Known Handwritten Draft of Martin Luther King Jr.’s ‘I Have a Dream’ Speech Could Top $10 M. at Christie’s

Christie’s announced Monday that it will offer the only known handwritten manuscript of Martin Luther King Jr.‘s 1963 speech at the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, better known as the “I Have a Dream” speech.

The manuscript has seven yellow pages of King’s handwriting, including edits and cross-outs. It will be offered in a single-lot sale on January 22, 2027. The lot will carry an estimate on request, though Christie’s said it expects the manuscript to sell for more than $10 million. Related Articles Rare Jan van Huysum Pendant Paintings Head to Christie's for $10.7 M. A Seagram Heir, a Bankrupt Hedge Funder, and More: Consignors for the November Marquee Sales Revealed

In a statement, Peter Klarnet, a manuscripts specialist at Christie’s, called the piece “a treasure of American history.”

“When I first saw these pages, and realized what they were, I was astounded,” Klarnet said. “It gives you chills to look at it. Reading along, you’re there in the moment with Dr. King, watching him compose it and making edits in real time. It captures a moment that literally changed the course of our nation and makes it very real and very human. It’s an honor and privilege that Christie’s has an opportunity to present it to the world.”

According to Christie’s, the pages were found in a desk drawer that belonged to Edward T. Clayton, head of public relations for the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC), the civil rights organization King led until his assassination in 1968. Clayton was also a speechwriter and editor for King and helped write the speech. His wife, Xernona Clayton, a civil rights leader and philanthropist, found the manuscript in the late 1990s. She recognized the speech but didn’t know it was the only handwritten final draft, so she put it back in her late husband’s desk. In 2024, she and her adviser, Eddie Bridgeman, brought the manuscript to Christie’s.

“I’m just glad I looked in the drawer,” Xernona Clayton said in a statement. “The two of them gelled with writing and words. They would go back and forth and there was such respect. Dr. King, who was a great thinker, said Ed was so good at getting his words on paper and putting them in the right place at the right time. I enjoyed watching them. I was privileged, and now the world will have the opportunity to see those words of wisdom that continue to inspire hope, freedom, and the pursuit of equality.”

The handwritten manuscript doesn’t include the words “I have a dream,” because King famously improvised that part of the speech. It does include his famous conclusion: “Free at last, free at last; thank God almighty, we are free at last.”

Christie’s said proceeds from the sale will go to charities “furthering the legacies of Ms. Clayton and Dr. King,” including the Xernona Clayton Foundation and the King Center in Atlanta.

“We are also grateful to join with Ms. Clayton to ensure that the sale of this draft helps support the great work of The King Center and our mother, Mrs. Coretta Scott King, who would be 100 this upcoming year,” Bernice A. King, the Kings‘ daughter, said in a statement.

The manuscript will be on view at the National Center for Civil and Human Rights in Atlanta from November 16–22. It will then be shown at Christie’s New York from January 15–21.

#9113. Anxiety Tattoos: How Ink Therapy Can Help Ease Mental Health Struggles

Tattoos have long been a flex in personal expression and artistry. For some peeps, they’re the go-to for commemorating life wins or solidifying deep-seated beliefs — from quotes that got you through dark times or portraits of your fave pets.

The act of getting inked can also be a profoundly therapeutic experience. The machine’s buzz and the needle’s sharp sting are part of a ritual that may help bring internal battles to the surface. But is there a link between anxiety and the decision to get tatted? Could framing your fears and anxieties in gorgeous designs help you cope? Continue reading to find out.

For many, tattoos are much more than art. Peeps who have anxiety may get tattoos as a way of taking control over their narrative, including their mental health struggles.

Anxiety disorder makes life challenging, and you may feel you’re stuck in a rip tide of continual worry, fear, and dread. Even if you know it’s the anxiety talking, you can still struggle to contain these overwhelming feelings, and it’s exhausting. Anxiety can trick your mind, tell you you’re unworthy, and there’s no way out.

But here’s where tattoos come into play — they create a visual shoutout to your strength and resilience. Imagine marking your skin with reminders of the battles you’ve won and what you’ve overcome.

Getting inked can feel like grabbing the reins back from anxiety and stress. A tattoo is an affirmation. It can turn your invisible battle scars into something tangible and beautiful, giving a sense of ownership over your body and experiences. This is huge when anxiety tries to convince you that you don’t have a say in your own story.

Whether it’s a poignant quote, a symbolic image, or just a badass design, a tattoo packs a punch of personal significance and your enduring strength. You’ve taken a deliberate, proactive step to help you take greater control over your life, and that should be celebrated.

Psychologically, tattoos are visual high-fives to yourself. For the anxious folks, tats are a way to take those messy, abstract feelings and pin them down in something real and tangible.

There’s also some evidence to suggest that the pain involved in tattooing can be cathartic, offering a physical release for emotional pain. This could explain why people who self-harm or live with substance misuse or eating disorders might be drawn to the tattoo chair — it’s a place where psychological pain is acknowledged and artistically transformed.

Research suggests there may be correlations between tattoos and mental health.

One 2013 study involving 65 female participants living with anorexia, bulimia, and binge eating disorder explored the relationship between eating disorders, self-injury, and tattoos. Around 51% of the participants reported a history of self-injury, and 27% had at least one tattoo. Those with tattoos were more likely to have a history of self-harm, so the authors suggested that tats could be a form of self-punishment.

However, in an interesting twist, 27% of those with tattoos showed no history of self-injury. These peeps reported more positive body image, higher self-esteem, and fewer mental health struggles.

The relationship between tats and mental health is complex and still being decoded. Further research would help confirm the link between the two.

Tattoos can swing either way on the mental health seesaw. For some folks, getting tattooed is symbolic of their healing process. It says, “Hey, I’ve been through some stuff, but look how I’ve grown!” These tattoos often become symbols of a deeply personal journey, spotlighting moments of triumph over anxiety and depression.

But here’s the flip side: if someone gets inked on a whim or during a rough patch without much thought, that tattoo could be a permanent reminder of a not-so-great time.

In a 2011 study of 82 peeps getting their first tattoo, researchers measured their feelings about their appearance and body both before they got the tattoo and then again immediately and three weeks after the tattooing. The findings showed that right after getting their tattoos, folks of all genders experienced a decrease in appearance anxiety and dissatisfaction. Three weeks later, they reported increased body appreciation, a stronger sense of having a distinctive appearance, heightened feelings of uniqueness, and improved self-esteem. However, female folks experienced increased anxiety related to how others viewed their physique 3 weeks post-tattoo, while males reported a decrease in this type of anxiety.

These results suggest that getting a tattoo can positively affect mental health, but of course, the impact varies among individuals.

Tattoos can be an artistic strategy to enhance your mental health game, but it’s crucial to take a beat and really think it through before you get inked.

Whether you’re looking to mark a milestone, manage the mayhem of anxiety, or remind yourself that everything will be okay, a carefully considered tattoo can be a meaningful addition to your narrative, helping you manage anxiety and positively shaping your story.

Unreal Engine 5.9 has received an early preview, and it's causing a bit of controversy among developers. The latest iteration of the platform that tops our pick of the best game development programs is all about AI, and that includes its own development.

The UE 5.9 Preview is Epic Games' first engine release built mainly via agentic workflows. A lot of the updates it introduces are also around AI-assisted workflows, including the use of Unreal MCP, Unreal Assistant and a new AI-driven content creation tool called Unreal Canvas.

The Unreal Engine 5.9 MegaJam Preview is here! It’s the first Unreal Engine release built primarily with agentic workflows and opens up a few new Experimental features: check out Unreal MCP’s expanded toolsets, work with AI coding agents directly in Editor, explore AI-assisted content creation, and run your projects in a browser. This isn’t your typical Unreal Engine Preview, but it’s ready just in time for the Epic MegaJam. Invite your agents and start experimenting: https://t.co/5WpPJnT4PWNovember 9, 2026

"Invite your agents," Epic tells developers in its announcement of the Unreal Engine 5.9 preview, highlighting the ability to work with AI coding agents directly in Editor and explore AI-assisted content creation.

Unreal Canvas is described as a shared workspace where people and agents create and refine content using Unreal Engine and the other connected tools. Its canvases include text, images, videos, and mesh generators that users can control with prompts and a chosen generation service.

The companion plugin Unreal Canvas Bridge exposes Movie Render Graph rendering to Canvas as MCP tools while Unreal Canvas Spatial Annotations places annotations in the 3D scene and captures the scene for use in Canvas.

Other updates in Unreal Engine 5.9 include improvements for animation, rendering and world-building with Lumen World Cache and improved Nanite culling. You can also run projects in browser again through WebAssembly and WebGPU.

Epic stresses that this isn't a conventional preview. It was put together in about a week for the 2026 Epic AI MegaJam, which runs from 12 to 15 November. It says the aim of the release is to learn how to build the engine with multiple people directing swarms of agents working in parallel. In addition, the timing seems intended to allow the jam to serve as a testing ground.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

"A handful of people directed fleets of agents to port the AI tooling from our UE6 development branch and implement Web as a target platform. Agents wrote the web platform code, starting from UE4's retired HTML5 platform, with engineers directing, reviewing, and testing the work," Epic says of how it developed the preview.

It adds: "we're already seeing benefits from this approach, and it allows us to deliver more UE5 releases with faster bug fixes and development on targeted features, all without pulling focus from UE6."

Unsurprisingly the heavy focus on AI is causing debate among developers. Those not interested in using AI agents are making a note to steer clear over concerns for the stability of the release. Epic has already clarified that some of the agent-written code still and parts of the web renderer are prototypes that will need to be cleaned up before the full release.

"I think we’ll just be staying on 5.8. LLMs are a great help, but literally everything about this preview sounds like something that crosses a boundary. Focus on optimising your code, what possessed you to add 3D model generation?" one person comments on X.

Others feels that Epic's approach is reasonable. "I'm not a fan of the asset gen stuff. But I do love more integration for agents! Including not trying to force us to use an agent IN the editor," on person argues.

Let us know what you think below. You can learn more on the website (also see our roundup of Unreal Engine tutorials and Unreal Engine courses).

#9111. Zohran Mamdani Visited MoMA’s West African Modern Architecture Survey and Loved It

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has continued his social media campaign to stump for exhibitions staged by the city’s museums, this time focusing on a survey of West African modernist architecture at the Museum of Modern Art, whose praises he sang on Instagram early this morning.

Titled “Architects of Liberation: Modernism in Western Africa,” the 400-work show surveys architectural projects in Senegal, Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, Togo, Benin, Nigeria, and Cameroon produced during a period of decolonization that began in some countries in the late 1950s. Curated by Martino Stierli and Ikem Stanley Okoye, the show features architectural models and archival imagery, as well as some contemporary artworks. Related Articles MoMA, Centre Pompidou, and M+ Will Treat Their Holdings as One Collection in Unprecedented Alliance MoMA to Stage Eva Hesse's First Major US Museum Exhibition in Two Decades

“visited @themuseumofmodernart this weekend and am still thinking about their exhibition ‘architects of liberation: modernism in western africa,’” wrote Mamdani in his post.

He specifically singled out Kader Attia’s 2014 sculpture Indépendence Tchao, a sculpture composed of rows of rusting index card boxes that the Algerian French artist obtained from a French colonial police headquarters. They are topped with a sign reading “HOTEL INDÉPENDENCE,” a reference to a similarly named hotel in Dakar, Senegal.

Mamdani wrote that the sculpture asks the question: “to what extent were the visions of the independence era achieved?”

It’s the second museum presentation Mamdani has posted about in the past month. In October, to celebrate his birthday, Mamdani visited the Studio Museum in Harlem, where he took in Taylor Simmons’s painting The Hypnotist (2026). Mamdani called the work by Simmons, a current participant in the museum’s storied artists-in-residence program, “just incredible.”

#9110. European Beauty Standards: Impact on Self-Image and Diversity

Though we see flickers of progress come and go, European beauty standards — which essentially worship white physical features as the best — are still prevailing across popular culture.

Keep reading to learn more about the damaging beauty ideal. Plus, hear from Siena Liggins, an independent artist and songwriter, about how it affects the music industry and what’s necessary for change.

European beauty standards focus on specific physical features, including light skin and eyes, thin bodies and noses, and poker-straight hair, to name a few.

“It’s honestly just a trickle effect of something that just exists in our culture on a very wide scale,” Liggins says about European beauty standards.

The Western ideal defines beauty through thinness and whiteness, something American culture was all about for, you know, ever.

But beauty standards often shift in America, moving from one extreme like the rail-thin “heroin chic” look in the 90s to today’s adoration of big butts and busts, with a focus on exercise.

Still, whiteness remains the most represented ideal, and we still obsess over thin bodies, regularly debating which celebrities may or may not be on weight loss medication.

The impression the European beauty standards leave us with is that those who most closely match the call for light skin and eyes, thin noses, etc., are the best or most attractive people — leaving some people of color to internalize the messaging, resulting in feelings of self-hate.

This Western beauty ideal is not only exclusionary — shutting out Black, Indigenous, Arab, and Asian, Pacific Islander people — but it’s also deeply harmful.

The standard is unmistakably splashed across the entertainment and beauty industries, from not finding your makeup shade to not seeing your features represented in media.

It also penetrates our daily work and play, creating societal issues and difficulty with self-esteem that impacts everything from securing and keeping a job to socializing and education, starting as young as nursery school.

For one workplace example, a 2020 study found that white women or Black women with straightened hair are more likely to land job interviews than Black women wearing natural hairstyles like afros, twists, curls, or braids.

Some of the first research on skin color and self-perception among Black children included “the doll test.” Researchers presented Black children, aged 3–7, with four dolls that all looked the same — except for their skin color — and asked them a series of questions about which dolls were nicest or prettiest and which they liked best.

Two-thirds of the Black children chose the white doll. The test was repeated in a similar way in 2005, with 16 of the 21 preschool-aged Black children selecting the white doll.

Needless to say, the beauty standard also negatively impacts the educational system, romantic relationships, and a slew of other dynamics and environments.

“The reality is that you need people to challenge them if you’re ever going to see anything change,” Liggins says about beauty standards.

She points to “AMERICAN REQUIEM,” one song off Beyoncé’s country album Cowboy Carter.

“She talks about how for things to stay the same, they have to change again,” Liggins explains. Though she believes Beyoncé refers to a hope for peace and healing in the United States, Liggins says this concept can lend to beauty standards.

When it comes to the idealistic view that we put on celebrities and pop culture, Liggins says you have to reimagine what it looks like over and over again. “And what that requires is letting in new people, and it can’t just be from a vanity’s perspective,” Liggins says.

Coupled with who is represented in music videos, Liggins says change is also needed at a gatekeeper level. “It has to be the people who are coming up with the ideas and bringing them into fruition who also have to have diversity, not just a thought but of background, culture, and ethnicity,” she says.

Otherwise, Liggins says, we’ll only continue to see spikes in diversity, making inclusion more of a fad than a serious change.

A Creative Agent, generative gap-fill, and a new approach to colour grading lead the way at Adobe Max.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Premiere Pro is getting Adobe's Creative Agent, and it looks set to take a lot of the grunt work out of editing. In a pre-Adobe Max 2026 demo, I saw it apply effects across every clip in a sequence, track masked subjects through frames, and adjust colour and exposure across an entire sequence at once. The use-case argument for more AI, now Agentic AI, in creative work, and particularly here in video editing, continues to be a replacement for repetitive jobs that most editors would happily hand off.

That, of course, raises questions about who used to be handed those repetitive but creative jobs and whether those roles are now no longer viable. But for many creatives, particularly freelancers, handing process work to an AI agent is likely very enticing.

So let's take a closer look at the new Generative Media Tool for those looking to speed up their workflows. Instead of jumping between apps and AI services, editors can generate video, sound effects, soundscapes, and music directly in Premiere's timeline. You can select a range, describe what you need, and add the generated media as an editable clip, so you don't have to break your editing flow to get the material you need. The demo was certainly impressive.

More controversially, Adobe is also bringing supported third-party AI models into the workflow, giving editors more choice in how they generate video but also opening up Adobe's app ecosystem to external AI models such as Kling and Seedance 2.5, which have greyer areas than Adobe Firefly. More practically, a new Generative Remove tool, currently in beta, can delete unwanted objects from a video frame and shot, filling the space with realistic detail, even figuring out where related shadows of a now-omitted object should be removed.

Color Mode is another big part of the Premiere Pro update. It's a dedicated colour-grading workspace that reshapes the interface around the job, with editable Style Presets that can apply a consistent look across an entire sequence. They're a bit like traditional Looks, only you can get inside them and adjust the individual elements.

You can also work across groups of clips, making it easier to fix inconsistencies between shots without grading each one individually. New on-screen HUDs provide feedback as you make adjustments, helping you stay focused on the footage rather than a wall of sliders.

Adobe is also expanding its AI-powered audio tools, including Enhance Audio, Separate Crosstalk, and Separate Sound Source, to clean up dialogue and separate elements in a mix.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Premiere Mobile is getting the Creative Agent in private beta, bringing agentic editing to phones. It can turn footage into editable first cuts, make changes using natural-language prompts and help refine videos while keeping the creator in control.

Adobe is also adding hundreds of thousands of licensed music tracks from Universal Music Group and Warner Music Group to Premiere Mobile on iPhone, with Android coming soon. There's a catch: the music is licensed for personal, non-commercial videos, while commercial projects can continue to use Adobe Stock Audio.

Finally, Premiere is included in Adobe's Local MCP integrations preview. This allows third-party agents to work with native Premiere project files locally, alongside Photoshop, Illustrator and After Effects. Importantly, sequences, bins and other project elements remain editable, meaning you can step in and make changes yourself.

As ever with these tools, the real test will be how much of the creative process editors are comfortable handing over.

#9108. Perrier-Jouët and Iris van Herpen partnership celebrates “biological processes that shape life”

Champagne house Perrier-Jouët has unveiled a creative collection with designer Iris van Herpen that draws on art nouveau design, soundscapes and the “invisible forces that shape the natural world”.

As part of the partnership, Van Herpen created Symphonic Bloom, a sculptural piece crafted from silk and recycled 22-carat gold.

The collectable sculpture was designed to delicately twirl up the neck of a Perrier-Jouët Belle Époque 1988 jeroboam champagne bottle. According to Van Herpen, it reflects “the unseen” and represents hidden entities, such as sound and energy frequencies.

During the piece’s creation, the designer recorded soundscapes of Perrier-Jouët’s champagne vineyards, documenting acoustic patterns via cymatics – a technology that makes sound waves visible via sand or water. The sculpture’s patterns are based on such vibrations.

“In nature, there is a silent yet ever-present dance of frequencies, rhythms, and biological processes that continuously shape life,” Van Herpen explained.

“The world is not only visual but vibrational – woven together by invisible forces that connect all living things,” the designer added.

The nature-informed element of the sculpture’s craft connects to Perrier-Jouët’s experimental regenerative viticulture programme, which aims to sustainably restore soil health across its vineyards.

Since 2021, the initiative has been successfully undertaken across 40 per cent of its sites.

This mirrors Van Herpen’s sustainability ethos, with the designer incorporating recycled materials into her designs and using techniques to minimise waste as much as possible.

In keeping with its multidisciplinary theme, Symphonic Bloom was also created to reflect the layered flavours of Perrier-Jouët Belle Époque cuvées and how they develop with time.

Alongside the sculpture, Van Herpen also produced Symphonic Life, a collectable edition of a Perrier-Jouët Belle Époque 1999 magnum, adorned in the botanical motifs seen in Symphonic Bloom.

Completing the set of collaborative cuvees is a bespoke version of Perrier-Jouët Belle Epoque 2018 that comes with a reimagined bottle and gift box, made in collaboration with cellar master Séverine Frerson.

“Inspired by the designer’s interplay of materials including metal, wood, silk and velvet, the cuvée reveals notes of white flowers, poached pear and grapefruit, lifted by a delicate touch of white pepper and a fine, silky finish,” said Séverine of Perrier-Jouët Belle Epoque 2018.

Perrier-Jouët explained that the collaboration with Van Herpen is built on a shared philosophy that spotlights and advocates for nature as a source of “inspiration, creation and transformation”.

“Treating nature as a collaborator, Iris van Herpen is one of fashion’s most forward-thinking designers, with a practice that reveals the invisible beauty of living systems, translating organic forces, micro-rhythms and subterranean life into visible form,” said Axelle de Buffevant, creative director of Perrier-Jouët.

De Buffévent explained that the shared mindset also mirrors its connections with the art nouveau movement, with which it has a long-standing cultural and artistic affinity.

The design movement’s reference was also interpreted by Van Herpen across the whole collaboration, where the movements of American dancer Loïe Fuller were also used as a source of inspiration across the project.

Fuller’s movements were used in art nouveau lamp design by French sculptor Raoul Larche, which is part of Perrier-Jouët’s extensive French art nouveau collection at Maison Belle Époque in Épernay.

The creations were presented on 21 October for Perrier-Jouët’s Banquet of Nature at The Peninsula Paris, which combined champagne, art and gastronomy into an interactive sensory gathering.

The project will continue its international journey in Miami, Florida, for the city’s design week in December 2026, of which the brand has a longstanding history.

“For many years, Perrier-Jouët and Design Miami have shared a commitment to creativity, craftsmanship and contemporary culture,” the brand said.

Perrier-Jouët is a partner of the fair and last year launched its Design for Nature Award, of which Van Herpen was the first recipient.

This year, during Design Miami, a final collaborative sculptural piece will be revealed, created by Van Herpen as the winner of the award.

The inscription adds, “We salute a leader who knows you can’t spell sacrifice without ‘I,’ and a warrior who reminds us that sometimes when you’re called to stand up, it’s best to just sit down and rest your feet.” The statue has been named The Foot Soldier.

The Foot Soldier is the latest work by the Secret Handshake, whose work has been taunting the president since 2024. On Monday, the group said that as Trump “continues to wage a war and threaten new ones, it’s time to harken back to a time when Donald Trump would do whatever it takes to stay out of combat.”

#9105. American Alliance of Museums Makes Case for Policy Proposals Following Democrats’ Landslide Election Win

Since President Donald Trump returned to office last year, his administration has made reining in the cultural sphere a core plank of his agenda.

Those efforts have included slashing federal funding for the National Endowment for the Humanities (NEH) and the National Endowment for the Arts (NEA); attempting to remake the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington, D.C., in his image; and unleashing a relentless barrage of executive orders, attempted firings, and investigations targeting the Smithsonian Institution and its affiliated museums. The campaign reached a fever pitch in July, when the White House released a 162-page report detailing supposed “ideological capture” at the National Museum of American History. Two congressional hearings followed, in which lawmakers grilled the museum’s director, Anthea Hartig, over her perceived failure to uphold the institution’s mission. Related Articles Nearly Everyone Is Concerned About How Museums Use AI in Exhibitions, Survey Says After a Museum Explores Homes Destroyed by US-Made Munitions, House Republicans Demand Information on Smithsonian's Curatorial Process

The American Alliance of Museums (AAM), a leading industry group for museums, has steadfastly defended cultural institutions facing Trump’s wrath, rebuking the administration’s efforts in public statements.

Now, with the political winds shifting and Democrats having secured their biggest midterm election victory in decades, AAM isn’t wasting time. In a statement released November 4, the day after the election, the organization said it plans to push the newly elected Congress to restore or increase funding for the Institute of Museum and Library Services (IMLS), as well as for the NEA and NEH. (Trump’s proposed 2025 budget would have decimated IMLS, but following an advocacy campaign led by AAM, and legal challenges from the American Library Association and the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, its budget was largely restored.) AAM also called for lifting the House Appropriations Committee’s current ban on earmark funding for museums.

Asked about the organization’s priorities for the incoming Congress, an AAM spokesperson told ARTnews, “We’re focused on continuing to build strong bipartisan support for museums, protecting federal funding for museums, and ensuring museums can fulfill their educational missions without political interference which is an important part of the conversation for the entire field.”

AAM did not offer details on how Congress might prevent political interference in the museum field. In late September, a group of Democratic lawmakers led by Representative Melanie Stansbury of New Mexico introduced a bill to protect the independence of the Smithsonian Institution, a measure AAM endorsed. At the time, Devon Akmon, chair of AAM’s board, said of the bill, “Protecting the Smithsonian’s scholarly independence honors that public trust and affirms a principle fundamental to all museums: scholarship and interpretation must be guided by evidence, expertise, and professional standards, not political influence.” The bill has not advanced since its introduction and will need to be reintroduced when the new Congress convenes in January.

On December 2, AAM will host a live webinar with Brandy Dillingham, its director of advocacy, and Nichole Westin, its senior director of government and field relations, on how the election results may affect museums.

#9103. Should I Exercise with a Phlegmy Cough? What You Need to Know

You’re feeling a bit under the weather, but you don’t want to lose the momentum of your fitness routine. So, should you push through and hit the gym, or is it better to rest and let your body heal? Let’s break it down!

Sleep is the best way to help your body recover quickly when you’re sick. But if you’re determined to rise and grind, you could use the “neck check” to decide whether to lace up those sneakers or stay in bed.

Many sports doctors use this theory to say that if your symptoms are above the neck — sniffles, sore throat, or a mild headache — you’re generally good to go for a light workout. But if you’re dealing with chest congestion, a hacking or juicy cough, diarrhea, a fever, or an upset stomach, it’s better to take some time to catch up on your Netflix watchlist.

Big disclaimer: there’s little scientific evidence behind the “neck check,” so use your best judgment.

If you’re going with the above-the-neck rule, exercising with the following symptoms is probably okay.

Going super hard if you have a mild cold is not a good idea. But a light workout, like a walk or a chill Peloton sesh, can be a great way to stay active without overdoing it. Stretching or light yoga might also do the trick.

Stick to light activities like walking for most earaches. Avoid intense workouts like weightlifting, yoga, or pilates, as they can throw off your balance and put pressure on your sinuses, exacerbating the pain.

Light and short workouts are likely fine if your sore throat is mild and lacks fever, cough, or swallowing issues. Remember to stay hydrated — it can ease your sore throat and is beneficial during exercise.

Light activities like brisk walks or gentle bike rides can help for allergy-related stuffy noses. If your nose is blocked, stick to very light activities, focusing on breathing. Skip workouts if you have a fever, chest congestion, or a productive cough with phlegm until you’re symptom-free.

If you’re experiencing the following symptoms, the workout can wait.

Working out with a fever increases dehydration risk and can worsen the fever. Plus, fever saps your muscle strength and coordination, making you more prone to injuries. So, do yourself a favor and skip the workout until you’re back to normal.

An occasional cough is your body’s way of clearing out irritants, but a frequent or phlegmy cough could signal a respiratory infection like a cold, flu, or even pneumonia or asthma. While a tickle-induced cough isn’t a gym deal-breaker, a persistent one is.

Diarrhea and vomiting can dehydrate you, and physical activity only makes that dehydration worse. Feeling weak? That’s a recipe for injury. Plus, stomach bugs are highly contagious. If you feel antsy, stick to light stretching or yoga at home.

The flu hits your respiratory system hard, with symptoms like fever, chills, sore throat, body aches, fatigue, headache, cough, and congestion. If you’ve got the flu, take it easy and give your body some well-earned R&R.

Once symptom-free, ease back into exercise gradually. Start with less intense workouts to avoid overdoing it. As your symptoms fade, you can gradually return to normal activity.

Regular exercise may shorten recovery time, particularly for acute respiratory infections. Listen to your body’s signals to gauge your strength. If you’re still contagious, opt for home or outdoor workouts, so you don’t spread those germs to fellow gym-goers.

#9102. SWA implements modular "toolkit" for a more walkable Houston

Photography by Bill Tatham unless otherwise stated

Landscape architecture studio SWA has organised a modular system that can be deployed around the city and includes mesh canopies designed by architecture studio Höweler + Yoon in an effort to create a more comfortable streetscape in Houston, Texas, USA.

The Cool & Connected Corridors project seeks to retrofit the streets of Houston with cooling infrastructure to create a more walkable pedestrian experience.

The project is part of Houston’s wider Public Realm Action Plan initiative aimed at making the urban streetscape “more delightful, comfortable and easy”, according to the city.

The network of architectural elements is designed to be integrated into varying, pre-existing sidewalk conditions, according to the team, and has been installed along a 15-block stretch of the city’s Texas Avenue as Phase 1 of the Public Realm Action Plan roll-out.

“Cool & Connected Corridors is a blueprint for taking action here and now, showing how cities can layer social, economic, and environmental benefits in a cost-efficient way,” said SWA principal Natalia Beard.

The “easily replicable toolkit” includes three main components – a lighting system aimed at improving visibility and safety at night, modular planting beds and mesh cooling pavilions designed by architecture studio Höweler + Yoon.

The petal-shaped pavilions are made of bead-blasted stainless steel, with mesh membranes in gradients of blue, green and purple.

They stretch up overhead, providing shade on street corners during the day, and integrated lighting illuminates them at night.

According to the team, they were designed to be installed as a single unit, or clustered together to form “bouquets”.

“Together, they create a sequence of shaded landmarks that help orient pedestrians from block to block,” said Höweler + Yoon co-founder Meejin Yoon.

The integrated lighting designed for the system is globe- and line-form lighting that drops down from the tree canopy.

According to the team, it was informed by a lighting study performed by the city in 2023, which identified a master plan for illuminating the nightime streetscape.

Other elements in the Cool & Connected Corridors system include wayfinding, replacement trees and a careful selection of drought-tolerant and pollinator-supportive plants throughout the planters.

The system along Texas Avenue was installed in the city ahead of the 2026 FIFA World Cup.

Since its installation, “thermal infrared readings of ground surfaces beneath the shade structures show an average temperature reduction of 10°F (5°C), with reductions of up to 30°F (16°C) in some locations”, said SWA.

Next, the city plans to install the system along the remaining portion of Texas Avenue and along other strips of the downtown area including McKinney Street and Preston Street.

Another recent urbanism project aimed at improving walkability is the pedestrianisation of Oxford Street in London.

Elsewhere in Houston, STG recently released renders of a twisting skyscraper, while the city is also set to receive projects by OMA and Theaster Gates.

#9101. Actor Says He Removed His Mother’s Art from Venice Biennale Installation as a Pro-Israel Protest

Actor Eric Rasmussen revealed this week that he had removed his contribution to an installation by Denniston Hill in the main exhibition of the Venice Biennale because the residency program appeared to support the “eradication” of Israel, in Rasmussen’s view.

In an op-ed published by the Jewish Journal on Monday, Rasmussen wrote that he had combined two drawings by his mother of Adolf Hitler drawn from a notebook she kept during her childhood. The resulting work, transferred to an acetate panel, was included Denniston Hill’s installation, an exquisite corpse–style work titled Chimera (2026) that is located in the Giardini section of Koyo Kouoh’s main exhibition. Related Articles French Artist Claude Lévêque Ordered to Stand Trial for Rape and Sexual Assault of Minors Venice Biennale President Stands by Decision to Host Russian Pavilion: 'I'd Do It All Over Again'

The piece features contributions by dozens of past residents at Denniston Hill, which was cofounded by artists kara lynch, Julie Mehretu, Paul Pfeiffer, and Jessica Rankin, along with art historian Lawrence Chua and curator Beth Stryker, and is located in Upstate New York. Rasmussen was a resident at Denniston Hill in 2019 through the DPAA Workshop.

Rasmussen said his submission to Chimera was a 1943 drawing by his mother that he had previously enlisted in a performance staged during his Denniston Hill residency. The piece is a drawing of a mustachioed man and some numbers, along with text reading, “Mister Hitler is invaded and his spitting.” For the Venice Biennale, he added a caption in red: “Mom’s childhood drawing 1943. The Toxicity of the Past?”

“I felt like the piece reflected the work I did at Denniston Hill while, at the same time, gesturing toward our current moment,” Rasmussen writes. “Neither the ‘toxicity’ of authoritarian leaders nor the rabid antisemitism called to mind by Hitler’s image remain in the past.”

ARTnews was able to confirm that the drawing did make it on view in time for the Biennale’s opening in May by examining installation shots of Chimera disseminated by the exhibition, which closes later this month.

It appears to have been taken away by Rasmussen at some point after mid-May, when, he wrote, Denniston Hill sent an email noting that the organization was more than 70 Biennale participants who had signed an open letter that objected to the Biennale’s claims of political neutrality. The signatories said this conflicted with the controversial decision this year to host pavilions for Israel, Russia, and the United States, all of which are “current regimes committing war crimes,” the letter said.

Moreover, according to Rasmussen, Denniston Hill wrote that it was “aligning with ANGA,” or the Art Not Genocide Alliance, a group that has repeatedly protested Israel’s presence at the Biennale while also noting that Palestine has no official pavilion in the show, and never has. (Palestine is not considered a state in Italy; only countries viewed as states by Italy’s government can have national pavilions at the Biennale, per the exhibition.)

“ANGA clearly considers all of Israel to be occupied Palestine and its goal is not to oppose policies of the government of Israel but to destroy the nation,” Rasmussen claimed in his Jewish Journal essay, which alleged that Denniston Hill has “no problem blithely aligning itself with an organization that seeks that nation’s eradication without even asking for the opinions of its artists.”

His essay also labeled anti-Zionism “an assault on not only the Jewish state and Jewish history, but also on language itself,” and claimed that linking “Zionism with racism, colonialism and apartheid” was akin to “Cold War KGB propaganda.”

Without stating a precise date for the work’s removal, Rasmussen said he “wrote a lengthy email” to Denniston Hill seeking the return of the drawing. Denniston Hill obliged the request and gave back the drawing, he said.

Representatives for Denniston Hill and the Biennale did not respond to requests for comment.

"Is Social Security taxable?" is one of the most common tax questions retirees ask — and the answer frustrates almost everyone: it depends. Depending on your total income, anywhere from 0% to 85% of your Social Security benefits can be subject to federal income tax. The tax was introduced in 1983, originally affecting about 10% of recipients. Today, because the income thresholds were never indexed for inflation, roughly 56% of Social Security recipients pay tax on their benefits.

The good news: even in the worst case, you'll never pay tax on 100% of your Social Security. The bad news: the formula for calculating the taxable amount is one of the most convoluted in the entire tax code. In this guide, we'll break it down into plain English, show you exactly how to calculate what you owe, and — most importantly — share strategies the FI community uses to reduce or eliminate the tax entirely.

The IRS uses a special formula called "combined income" (also called "provisional income") to determine how much of your Social Security benefits are taxable. Here's the formula:

Combined Income = Adjusted Gross Income (AGI) + Nontaxable Interest + Half of Social Security Benefits

The resulting number determines which taxation tier you fall into. Notice that the thresholds haven't changed since 1993 — they are not adjusted for inflation, which means more retirees cross into taxable territory every year.

Important: "Up to 85% taxed" does not mean you pay an 85% tax rate. It means 85% of your benefits are added to your taxable income and taxed at your ordinary income rate. If you're in the 22% bracket and 85% of your $30,000 benefit is taxable, you'd owe 22% on $25,500 — roughly $5,610.

This is the most common Social Security tax confusion. When the IRS says "up to 85% of benefits are taxable," it means 85% of your benefit amount gets added to your taxable income and taxed at your regular rate. If your marginal rate is 22% and 85% of your $30,000 benefit is taxable, you owe about $5,610 — not $25,500. The effective tax rate on your full benefit in this example is about 18.7%.

Let's walk through a real example. Meet Sarah: she's 67, single, retired, and receives $24,000 per year in Social Security benefits. She also has $18,000 in IRA withdrawals and $2,000 in municipal bond interest.

Step 2: Determine the Tier Sarah is single with combined income of $32,000, which falls between $25,000 and $34,000. She's in the 50% tier — up to 50% of her benefits may be taxable.

Step 3: Calculate the Taxable Amount The actual calculation involves comparing two formulas and taking the lesser amount. For the 50% tier:

Sarah adds $3,500 to her other taxable income. At a 12% marginal rate, that's roughly $420 in additional federal tax on her Social Security.

Beyond federal taxes, 13 states also tax Social Security benefits to some degree as of 2026. Each state has its own thresholds and exemption amounts:

The remaining 37 states and Washington, D.C. do not tax Social Security benefits at all. If you're planning where to retire, this is a meaningful factor — especially if you have substantial SS benefits combined with other retirement income.

The FI community has identified several strategies that can significantly reduce the tax bite on Social Security benefits. The key insight: since taxation is based on combined income, controlling your income in retirement is the lever.

This is the single most powerful strategy. Roth IRA withdrawals are not included in the combined income formula. If you retire early (before Social Security age), you have a window of low-income years to convert Traditional IRA/401(k) money to Roth.

Example: Between ages 55 and 67, you convert $500,000 from your Traditional IRA to a Roth — paying tax at rates as low as 10-12%. When you claim Social Security at 67, your Roth withdrawals don't push you into a higher SS taxation tier. Instead of 85% of your benefits being taxable, you might pay tax on 0-50%.

The math is dramatic over a 25+ year retirement. Converting at 12% during early retirement to avoid 22%+ taxation on Social Security for decades produces enormous tax savings.

Every dollar of AGI pushes you toward the 50% or 85% taxation tiers. Strategic levers include:

Once you reach age 70.5, you can donate up to $105,000 per year directly from your IRA to a qualified charity. This satisfies your Required Minimum Distribution (RMD) without the distribution being included in your AGI. Lower AGI means lower combined income, which means less Social Security is taxable.

For charitably inclined retirees, QCDs are one of the most tax-efficient giving strategies available — they simultaneously reduce your income tax AND reduce the tax on your Social Security benefits.

Delaying Social Security from 62 to 70 increases your benefit by roughly 77%. But there's a secondary benefit: during the delay years, you have more room to do Roth conversions at low tax rates without Social Security benefits adding to your combined income. The combination of larger benefits and lower taxation on those benefits makes delay doubly powerful for tax optimization.

If you retire before claiming Social Security, you have a golden window for Roth conversions. With little or no earned income and no SS benefits, you can convert Traditional IRA money to Roth at the lowest tax brackets of your lifetime. Every dollar you convert is a dollar that will never increase the tax on your Social Security benefits. This window closes permanently once you start claiming.

A step-by-step walkthrough for estimating what you owe.

List your AGI from all sources: IRA/401(k) withdrawals, pension income, wages, dividends, capital gains, rental income. Get your total Social Security benefit from your SSA-1099 form.

Pro tip: Don't forget nontaxable municipal bond interest — it counts in the combined income formula even though it's not on your 1040.

Add your AGI + nontaxable interest + half of your Social Security benefits. This "combined income" number determines your taxation tier.

Compare your combined income to the thresholds: Single — $25K (50% tier), $34K (85% tier). Married filing jointly — $32K (50% tier), $44K (85% tier).

For the 50% tier: take 50% of combined income above the lower threshold (capped at 50% of benefits). For the 85% tier: the calculation is more complex — use IRS Publication 915 worksheet or tax software.

Pro tip: Tax software handles this automatically. If doing it by hand, IRS Publication 915 has the complete worksheet.

The taxable portion of your Social Security gets added to your other taxable income and taxed at your marginal rate. Check if your state also taxes Social Security.

For single filers, Social Security becomes partially taxable when combined income exceeds $25,000 (50% tier) and up to 85% taxable above $34,000. For married filing jointly, the thresholds are $32,000 (50% tier) and $44,000 (85% tier). These thresholds have not changed since 1993 and are not indexed for inflation.

No. Social Security benefits are not earned income. They are classified as unearned income for tax purposes. This distinction matters for things like the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC), IRA contribution eligibility, and the Social Security earnings test (which only applies to earned income like wages and self-employment).

No — and this is why Roth accounts are so powerful in retirement. Roth IRA withdrawals are not included in the combined income formula used to determine Social Security taxation. Converting Traditional IRA money to Roth before claiming Social Security can dramatically reduce the tax on your benefits for life.

Yes. File Form W-4V with the Social Security Administration to have federal income tax withheld from your benefits. You can choose 7%, 10%, 12%, or 22% withholding. This avoids the surprise of a large tax bill at filing time. State tax withholding varies by state.

Social Security benefits are included in the Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI) calculation that determines Medicare Part B and Part D premium surcharges (IRMAA). High-income retirees can pay significantly more for Medicare — up to 3.4 times the standard premium. Managing MAGI in retirement affects both Social Security taxation and Medicare costs.

There have been numerous proposals to reform Social Security taxation, including indexing the thresholds for inflation, raising the taxable percentage above 85%, or eliminating the tax entirely. As of 2026, no changes have been enacted. The thresholds have remained unchanged since 1993, meaning inflation automatically pushes more retirees into taxable territory each year.

Yes, Social Security benefits can be taxable — up to 85% of your benefits may be added to your taxable income depending on your combined income. The thresholds are low ($25,000 single, $32,000 married) and haven't been adjusted for inflation since 1993, catching more retirees every year. The single most powerful strategy is Roth conversions during early retirement years before claiming Social Security. Every dollar in a Roth account is a dollar that won't push your Social Security into the taxable zone. Plan your retirement income sources deliberately, and you can reduce or eliminate this tax entirely.

#9099. Does Creatine Increase DHT? What You Need to Know

Ah, creatine! It’s a popular supplement promising muscle gains and enhanced performance. But as you’re hitting the gym harder and seeing results, there are some potential side effects to be aware of. Here’s the lowdown.

Creatine monohydrate is a naturally occurring substance found in muscle cells. It helps to produce adenosine triphosphate (ATP) — your muscles’ go-to fuel when working hard.

Although you can find creatine in foods like red meat and seafood, many gym enthusiasts and athletes boost their stores with supplements. Why? Because more creatine equals more ATP, which means more energy for high-intensity activities. More fuel means more mileage!

Now, here’s where things get hairy. You might dial up your body’s DHT (dihydrotestosterone) production when you uplevel creatine. DHT is a derivative of testosterone and plays a big-league role in developing male characteristics. But here’s the catch: while DHT might beef up your alpha vibe, it’s also notorious for thinning out hairlines in peeps predisposed to male pattern baldness.

So, do creatine supplements cause baldness? Maybe! The buzz mainly stems from a small 2009 study where college-aged rugby players loaded up on creatine and saw their DHT levels increase significantly.

Because DHT can shrink hair follicles and shorten the hair growth cycle, it may seem logical to blame creatine for contributing to hair thinning. However, it’s important to remember that these findings are a one-hit wonder — they haven’t been seen again in other studies. Plus, let’s not forget that intense workouts alone can pump up these hormones, too.

As a result, the jury’s still out, making the creatine-and-baldness saga a hot topic for gym gossip and scientists alike.

The same 2009 study found that after a week of taking high-dose creatinine at 25 grams per day, DHT levels rose by 56%. When the researchers dropped the dose to 5g daily for two more weeks, levels remained 40% higher than baseline. These findings contrasted with the control group participants who took a placebo.

Does this mean creatine could spell disaster for your do? Well, creatine boosts DHT, the usual suspect in male pattern baldness, also called androgenic alopecia. However, your disposition to hair loss and the effects of DHT is genetic, meaning that it’s inherited.

Some folks are more prone to DHT’s hair-ruffling effects because of how their androgen receptor gene is wired. Hormones like testosterone and DHT bind to androgen receptors, typically triggering normal hair growth. However, variations in the AR gene make the androgens extra effective, making you more likely to experience hair loss.

So, while there isn’t much evidence to say that creatine supplements cause hair loss, the connection to increased DHT levels is worth considering if your family reunions look like a convention for bald eagles.

Beyond the potential for a breezy scalp, creatine is actually solid in the safety department, with long-term studies giving it a thumbs up. However, although creatinine doesn’t pose a risk to healthy individuals, it might not be your best move if you have kidney, high blood pressure, or liver disease.

Another thing to keep in mind is that creatinine loves to hang onto water, so expect some extra bloat and weigh-in surprises as your body adjusts.

Thinking of starting a creatine kick? Chatting with your doctor first is always wise, especially if you have other health conditions or take medications. They can advise you and rule out any potential interactions.

If you’re taking creatinine and notice changes to your hair, a check-up is a good idea. Shedding a few strands is normal, but it’s a red flag if you start losing clumps of hair. Rapid hair loss can indicate underlying health issues that go beyond your hairstyle.

Furthermore, consult a doctor if hair loss is weighing on your mind. They can offer solutions or treatments to manage your hair loss and stress.

Creatine is celebrated for its muscle-building prowess, but rumors of a link with hair loss exist. The good news is there’s little conclusive evidence directly connecting creatine supplementation to permanent hair loss.

However, creatine loading may boost DHT levels, a hormone linked to male pattern baldness, especially in people genetically predisposed to hair thinning.

So, if you’re concerned about hair loss, it might be wise to talk with a doctor before adding creatine supplements to your muscle-building routine.

#9097. Oxford University Museum Returns 39 Sets of Ancestral Remains to Naga People of India

At a ceremony held on November 9, the Pitt Rivers Museum at Oxford University in the UK formally returned 39 sets of ancestral remains to the Naga people of India. The remains, primarily human skulls, were taken during the British colonial rule of India and Burma (now Myanmar) and have been in the museum’s collection for more than 100 years. A delegation of almost 30 community members from Nagaland, an Indian state bordering Myanmar, traveled to Britain for the handover.

The Pitt Rivers claims to hold the largest collection of Naga artifacts in the world, most of which were acquired by John Henry Hutton, an anthropologist and colonial administrator in the Indian Civil Service, and a second administrator/anthropologist, James Philip Mills, between 1910 and 1940. Within that collection, 219 items are listed as Naga human remains, including 39 ancestral human remains and 178 objects that contain, or may contain, human hair. (The current return concerns only the 39 ancestors.) Related Articles Sweden Returns Benin Bronze Trove to Nigeria, Indigenous Remains to Bolivia Museum Wiesbaden Will Be Germany's First Institution to Return Colonial-Era Human Remains to Indonesia

On its website, the museum notes that colonial “collecting” was “often bound up with the structures of colonial violence; remains and objects were frequently confiscated during punitive military expeditions, rather than freely given.” Mills, who wrote three monographs on Naga culture and practice, refers to at least one armed expedition to demand “headhunting trophies” from Pangsha village, remarking that the Pitt Rivers would thus “get some fine specimens.”

While the Naga people practiced headhunting at the time, taking the severed heads of enemies as trophies, they also kept and cared for the heads of their own chiefs. According to anthropologist Dolly Kikon (a member of Nagaland’s Lotha-Naga community, now at the University of California, Santa Cruz) one of the remains being returned is a chief’s skull.

The Pitt Rivers removed all human remains, including those of Naga people, from display in 2020, publicizing the removal. Sensing an opening, Kikon contacted the museum’s director, Laura Van Broekhoven and offered to connect her with the Naga community. The return is the culmination of the museum’s six-year collaboration with Naga partners, which included the Forum for Naga Reconciliation (FNR) together with tribal Hohos, elders, churches and communities.

Naga tribal leaders plan to bury the remains together in a joint memorial park. “They’ve been here in a foreign land for more than a century,” said Dr Vihuto Asumi, President of the Sumî Hoho Naga tribe. “We believe that their spirits are still not at rest, so by doing this, we believe it will bring spiritual healing, not only to the ancestral remains here but to everyone who died during the headhunting days.”

#9096. 4Space draws on cultural significance of Arabian horses for UAE restaurant

Design studio 4Space “explored the physical and kinetic qualities” of horses for the fluid, organic design of Falwa, an Abu Dhabi restaurant celebrating modern Emirati cuisine.

Located in the Abu Dhabi Royal Equestrian Art (ADREA) academy, the contemporary restaurant is led by Michelin-starred Emirati chef Faisal Alharmoodi.

To showcase the importance of the Arabian mare as a cultural icon in this equestrian space, 4Space designed the restaurant to represent abstract depictions of horses and their anatomy.

“The design team explored the physical and kinetic qualities of the animal itself, specifically its skeletal structure, muscular tension, and fluid movement,” 4Space said.

It aimed to convey the animal’s cultural and historical importance through architecture, using an organic design language throughout the restaurant, which fittingly opened in 2026 – the Year of the Horse.

Named Falwa after the Arabic term for a young female mare in her first year of life, the eatery has a fluid interior with stretched, curved walls designed to evoke horses in motion.

The restaurant interior also references a specific horse named Rabdan, the late Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan’s, which inspired the custom-made dusty white mineral plaster that wraps its walls and adds a tactile feel.

“This earthier, softer alternative to pure white acts as a passive canvas for the shifting daylight, allowing natural and artificial light to paint dynamic shadows across the curved walls, evoking the powerful presence and coat of the horse,” 4Space explained.

Rabdan’s coat also influenced Falwa’s overall colour palette, which features warm reddish, tan and brown hues against the white walls.

“By utilising rich crimson tones and warm, tactile materials, the design team evokes the powerful presence and coat of this legendary steed,” 4Space explained.

Falwa’s tactile, organic feel of the walls is contrasted by the polished, glossy flooring, which was made from Breccia Aurora marble. Its beige and brown veining matches the restaurant’s earthy brown leather and wood tones.

While the restaurant mostly features abstract references to Arabian horses, 4Space also added more specific equestrian details to the interior.

4Space created custom-made dining chairs with decorative leather straps, visible stitching and metal hardware in a nod to horse saddles and tack.

Above the central tables at the restaurant, a tactile sculpture with a skeletal, undulating design once again evokes movement and anatomy.

4Space also used the Vibia Plusminus lighting system by designer Stefan Diez for Falwa. Its signature textile straps, from which glass globes are suspended, match the equestrian leather straps on the chairs and add a playful effect to the interior.

Overall, 4Space aimed to tie Falwa’s food and interior together, with both aspects of the restaurant functioning as contemporary expressions of Emirati culture and heritage.

“The design demonstrates how a deep cultural relationship can be expressed as a living, modern architectural language,” the studio concluded.

#9095. 10 Signs You Might Not Really Be in Love: How to Tell the Difference

Love can feel like navigating a choose-your-own-adventure book with half the pages missing. Are you truly in love or just caught in a wave of infatuation? Sometimes, what seems like a heart-thumping romance may be a fleeting crush.

Wondering how to tell the difference? We’ve got you! Here’s a rundown of the 10 signs you’re not really in love.

Feeling a bit puzzled about your feelings for boo? That’s pretty normal. But before you start planning your future or picking out matching Halloween costumes, you may wanna make sure it’s real love and not a case of a serious crush.

Here are some signs that you may not really be in love:

Caught up in the romance novel vibe? If you’re all about the feelings of being in love rather than who’s sharing your popcorn, it might just be that you’re smitten with the idea of love itself.

Time to check if your relationship is more about the fairy tale than the real person.

Chatting with your partner shouldn’t feel as shallow as a kiddie pool. If deep talks are tougher than pulling teeth and rarer than a unicorn, it’s a red flag.

Sticking to small talk about the weather and dinner plans suggests the emotional depth for a lasting bond might be missing.

When discussions about future plans feel as far-fetched as sci-fi adventures, they may reveal underlying doubts about the relationship’s viability.

If imagining a future together feels unrealistic or undesirable, it’s time to ask yourself why. Real love plans a future; infatuation lives for the weekend.

Remember when their sock on the floor was cute? If little quirks now make you more cranky than charmed, it might mean the love goggles are off, your feelings have shifted from affection to annoyance, and the reality check has bounced.

Love is seeing imperfections and adoring them anyway.

Feeling more at ease or more ‘yourself’ when your partner isn’t around is a telling sign. If you’re secretly throwing mini-parties when they leave the room, you need to stop and think. Real-deal love means missing their chaos when they’re gone, not celebrating the silence.

Shared values are the anchor of deep, lasting relationships. If your core values clash more than a polka dot and stripes ensemble, you’re in for a rough ride, as finding common ground could be challenging!

Lasting love grows from shared beliefs and mutual respect, not from opposing battle lines.

No respect? No future. Respect is as critical to love as air is to breathing. Without mutual respect, you might just be coexisting rather than genuinely connecting.

If you no longer admire or respect each other’s opinions and choices, sustaining a healthy relationship will be difficult.

If they’re out of sight and totally out of mind, that’s not just independence — it might be indifference. When love is real, you should long for their laugh or lame jokes when they’re away. Could it be that your emotional attachment isn’t as strong as it should be for a lasting relationship?

If your best moments are consistently away from your partner, your heart might not be in it to win it. Perhaps your relationship isn’t providing enough support or happiness.

True love enriches your life and doesn’t play second fiddle to your social circle. It’s time to evaluate where your emotional energy is invested.

Still window shopping while you’re supposedly locked down? It’s a sign you might not be all in. A love that lasts doesn’t keep a backup catalog — it’s too busy loving what it already has.

Knowing why you’re still scanning for alternatives can help you address what might be missing or unfulfilled in your relationship.

Are you genuinely in love or just in love with being in love? If you’re secretly thrilled when they’re not around, stuck in surface-level chit-chat, or dreading deep-future talks, these are cosmic signs that it’s rethink o’clock.

Don’t ignore the signals — tuning in now can save you heartache later and lead you toward a love that genuinely fulfills you.

Last medically reviewed on June 26, 2024

#9094. Man Who Discovered Renaissance Church Facade Hidden in His House to Receive €1 M. Reward

When Juan Francisco León Catena bought an old house in southern Spain, he expected that a planned renovation would incur costs. What he came to learn was that a Renaissance church facade was hidden behind the walls—and that it came with a reward worth more than €1 million ($1.2 million).

The discovery dates to November 2016, when León Catena and his father began tearing down interior walls in a property he’d purchased in Úbeda, a historic town in Andalusia that, together with neighboring Baeza, was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2003. Behind the plaster and partitions, they found an enormous stone facade measuring roughly 49 feet wide and 36 feet tall. Related Articles Three Works of Sacred Art Stolen From Spanish Churches as Authorities Warn of Rise in Art Theft $1.98 M. Worth of Gold Pieces Stolen From the Treasure of Villena

The stonework turned out to be part of the chapel of the former Hospital of San Jorge, also known as the Hospital of Pero Almindes, which was founded in 1347. The surviving facade includes Renaissance additions attributed to Andrés de Vandelvira, the 16th-century architect responsible for some of the region’s most celebrated buildings.

According to El País, heritage officials who examined the discovery praised its remarkable state of preservation and artistic value, describing it as a rare example of Renaissance funerary chapel architecture.

The discovery also brought León Catena’s renovation plans to a halt. Under Spanish heritage law, the facade is protected, meaning any alterations to the property are subject to strict restrictions. But the same legislation, passed in 1985, also provides financial rewards for people who accidentally discover historically significant objects or structures during construction or demolition work.

Getting that reward proved more complicated than finding the facade.

The regional government initially refused to pay, setting off a legal battle that dragged on for years. Spain’s Supreme Court has now settled the dispute in León Catena’s favor. Now, nearly a decade after the discovery, an Andalusian government valuation committee has determined that León is entitled to more than €1 million. He has yet to receive the money.

The monument itself, meanwhile, remains in limbo. León Catena has been negotiating with local officials over a plan to expose the facade to the street, allowing residents and tourists to see it. In exchange, he has proposed that the city cover the cost of renovating the four-story building.

But time may be running out. A conservation report commissioned by the regional government warned that leaking roofs in adjoining municipal properties have caused water damage, rotting wooden beams, and mold. The deterioration, officials said, could eventually lead to a structural collapse.

“Every month that passes without action increases the concern,” León Catena told El País, adding that the authorities have been warned about the risks but have yet to agree on a solution.

For now, the facade is cordoned off, essentially as it was when León Catena discovered it in 2016. He and his family, who had originally hoped to make the building their home, have since moved into another building on the same street.

“Too much time has passed,” León Catena said. His priority now, he added, is to make the long-hidden monument accessible to the public.

When KitBash bought ArtStation, it pledged the address users concerns about the flood of AI content on the digital art platform. It took the first step back in September, when it turned on 'NoAI' for uploads by default, marking them as unavailable for AI training.

Now a new update introduces an attempt to police generative AI content along with more complete AI declarations and more control over filtering. The aim is to make it easier to users to control what they see, but it's got a mixed response from artists so far.

We're introducing the next phase of generative AI content controls. Creators will have clearer AI declaration requirements when publishing, and AI filtering is now on by default, with options that give you finer control. Learn what's changing → https://t.co/cuHmcoAuhw https://t.co/64PevA0XjmNovember 9, 2026

When publishing content on ArtStation, users will now be asked to declare whether generative AI was used in the creation of the piece. Creators can identify their work as primarily generative AI, mixed generative AI and non-generative methods or 100% non-generative.

This relies on users being upfront, and ArtStation says that most are. However, it's recognised that there is a problem with people uploading AI-generated content without flagging it as such.

That leads to the second aspect of the latest update, which is a dedicated channel for reporting AI content. If users come across artwork they think is AI-generated but which isn't labelled, they can report it. ArtStation says that every report will help improve its AI filtering for the whole community.

Users also get more control over what they're shown: they can choose whether to hide declared generative AI content, or to allow mixed generative and non-generative workflows, and they can adjust how aggressively ArtStation filters content based on user reports of suspected generative AI.

The 'Strict' setting hides artwork when just a few reports suggest it may be AI-generated. 'Balanced' filters it out when there’s a moderate level of reports and 'Loose' removes it only when user signals are strongest. By default, the filter will be set to not show any project declared as AI-generated, tagged with 'CreatedwithAI' or tagged with generative AI tools, and suspected as AI will be set to strict.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

The platform risks becoming useless if it's impossible to find interesting work because of the sheer volume of low-quality AI-generated content. Many users have welcomed the latest update as a move in the right direction, while others have raised doubts about how effective the measures it will be.

There's a strong reliance on user moderation, which will depend on users accurately identifying AI art. Some may still go undetected completely, while the 'Strict' filtering could remove work falsely identified as AI.

It's not yet clear if artists will be notified if their work is flagged or whether they will have a way to contest that decision. That could be a concern when even long established digital artists like Loish have been falsely accused of using AI over on platforms like TikTok.

The update highlights the difficult balancing act of policing AI content. ArtStation has a big focus on concept art, and some in the industry now see generative AI as an inevitable part of the pipeline in this field. The new Disney deal with Adobe will focus on developing custom AI models specifically for concept work. In that context, KitBash probably sees banning AI art from the platform as counterproductive if not impossible.

#9092. Nothing but a single joint holds together Dado furniture

Berlin studio Allen Kaufmann Architekten has adapted a traditional woodworking joint to create a flat-pack range that can be assembled completely without tools – and it’s been voted furniture design of the year by Dezeen readers.

No glue, screws, brackets or other fasteners are used in the Dado tables and shelves.

Instead, their solid-timber construction is held together using only one deceptively simple type of joint: a narrow trench cut across the length of one piece of wood so another can slot into it.

Known as a dado or housing joint, it has been a fixture of woodworking for thousands of years.

But Allen Kaufmann Architekten has reimagined this traditional technique as the only thing holding up an entire self-supporting furniture range that can be easily flat-packed, assembled, demounted and repaired.

“I started with the traditional dado cut, a simple groove cut into timber, and asked whether that basic operation could become an entire structural system rather than simply a joint,” explained studio co-founder Justin Allen.

His patented joint, developed over several years of prototyping, turns dado cuts on their head – or more precisely, at a 45-degree angle – so they can be used to join not just two pieces of wood but four.

This allows a vertical element, a horizontal element and two diagonal braces to lock together at a single point through simple geometry.

“Visually, it has something of a post-and-beam construction, with intersecting diagonal bracing, almost like the inside of a timber barn,” the architect explained. “But the geometry and the way all four elements meet are specific to Dado, giving the joint its own distinct appearance.”

So far, Allen has used this same logic to create a table and a modular shelving system, using a limited set of repeated parts.

As Allen sees it, this offers a more elegant solution to current joinery systems. Furniture with permanent fixings is cumbersome, expensive and emissions-intensive to transport, he argues, while traditional flat-pack systems rely on different screws, brackets and fittings that can be lost or damaged.

In both cases, the joints limit how often and how easily the furniture can be disassembled and reused, which can lead to an otherwise functional piece being abandoned.

With Dado, Allen has avoided the need for fixings and left the joints themselves exposed, in the hope that the furniture’s owner will be able to understand how it works and how it might be maintained.

“The connection remains visible, so the joint becomes the detail, the structure, the assembly and ultimately the design,” he explained.

Each of the range’s standard components is CNC milled with machine precision. This allows the whole range to be produced by a single workshop anywhere in the world – another win in the transport department.

Dado was named furniture design of the year in this year’s Dezeen Awards public vote and is now in the running to be crowned overall winner by a jury of leading industry figures including Norman Foster, Michael Anastassiades and Jaime Hayon.

#9091. Museum Organizations Call Bipartisan Infrastruture Bill a ‘Sweeping Assault’ on Historic and Sacred Places

Some historic preservationists are alarmed at the potential effects of a bipartisan bill whose sponsors say it aims to cut red tape for infrastructure and energy production projects.

On Monday, the US Senate advanced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (S.5653), introduced by Senator Shelley Moore Capito, a West Virginia Republican, by a vote of 73–25. The bill is cosponsored by Senators Mike Lee, a Utah Republican; Sheldon Whitehouse, a Rhode Island Democrat; and Martin Heinrich, a New Mexico Democrat. (The current session of the Republican-controlled Senate runs through December 18; new senators will be sworn in on January 3.) Related Articles American Alliance of Museums Makes Case for Policy Proposals Following Democrats' Landslide Election Win Nearly Everyone Is Concerned About How Museums Use AI in Exhibitions, Survey Says

Crucially, the act would narrow the scope of the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA), in part by limiting which types of projects trigger review.

Speaking on the Senate floor Monday, Capito said that “for far too long, critical investments in our nation’s infrastructure, energy production, and economy have been forced to sit on the sidelines due to endless red tape, duplicative reviews, and regulatory uncertainty.” Data from the National Association of Manufacturers, she said, “shows that permitting delays are costing America’s manufacturers $12.1 billion every year, including $87 million in additional costs in West Virginia alone. According to new data from McKinsey, $1.8 trillion of investments are locked up in the federal permitting system right now, including $22.3 billion of sidelined investments in my home state of West Virginia.”

According to the Art Newspaper, about 800 protesters gathered on the West Lawn of the US Capitol, among them leaders from the Association of African American Museums, the DC Preservation League, the American Institute of Architects, and the Archaeological Institute of America. Representative Melanie Stansbury, a New Mexico Democrat, called the act a “dirty deal.” Critics cited by the paper noted that the senators introduced the 500-page bill just 48 hours before the Senate vote was scheduled.

S.5653 targets Section 106 of the NHPA, which requires federal agencies to consider the impact of federally funded building projects and requires those receiving federal funds or permits to consult with tribal nations. According to the Art Newspaper, the new bill would make consultation with tribal nations optional and remove the requirement that federal agencies notify and consult with the public and tribal nations about potential harm to historic sites. It would also narrow the definition of what constitutes a historic site.

On November 6, the 106 Strong Coalition, which includes more than 1,200 organizations, tribal nations, and advocates, sent a letter to Congress calling for the defeat of S.5653. Signatories include the American Alliance of Museums, numerous state museum associations, and many individual museums. The letter calls the bill “a sweeping assault on the protections Congress enacted sixty years ago to ensure that federal agencies consider the consequences of their decisions for America’s historic and sacred places.”
